Problem: A $2\text{ kg}$ block moving at $6\text{ m/s}$ makes a head-on elastic collision ($e = 1$) with a stationary $1\text{ kg}$ block. Calculate the final velocity of the $1\text{ kg}$ block after the collision.

Solution:

  1. Apply elastic collision velocity formula for second body: $v_2 = \frac{2 m_1 u_1 + (m_2 - m_1) u_2}{m_1 + m_2}$.
  2. Substitute initial values ($m_1 = 2\text{ kg}, u_1 = 6\text{ m/s}, m_2 = 1\text{ kg}, u_2 = 0$):
  3. Calculate $v_2$: $v_2 = \frac{2(2)(6) + 0}{2 + 1} = \frac{24}{3} = 8\text{ m/s}$.

JEE/NEET Key Takeaways

  • Work done by centripetal forces is always zero because the force vector remains perpendicular to velocity vector at every instant ($\vec{F} \perp \vec{v}$).
  • Area under a Force-Displacement ($F-x$) graph represents work done, while area under a Power-Time ($P-t$) graph represents total energy transferred.

fields.title: Oscillations & SHM: Complete Formula Sheet for JEE and NEET
fields.summary: Master differential equations, energy distribution, simple and compound pendulums, and spring-mass combinations
fields.content:
Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM) is a foundational oscillatory system where a restoring force directly proportional to displacement drives motion about a central equilibrium point. Mastering angular frequency, energy transformations, spring systems, and pendulum variations is crucial for high exam scores.

1. Kinematics & Differential Equation of SHM

An oscillating system undergoes simple harmonic motion when its acceleration is directly proportional to its displacement from equilibrium and directed toward that equilibrium position.

$$\frac{d^2 x}{dt^2} + \omega^2 x = 0 \implies x(t) = A \sin(\omega t + \phi)$$

  • Displacement, Velocity & Acceleration: Velocity leads displacement by $\pi/2$ phase ($v = \omega \sqrt{A^2 - x^2}$), while acceleration leads displacement by $\pi$ phase ($a = -\omega^2 x$).
  • Time Period & Frequency: System oscillation frequency depends on angular velocity via $T = \frac{2\pi}{\omega} = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}$.
  • Phase Relationship: Maximum velocity occurs at mean position ($x = 0$, $v_{max} = A\omega$), whereas maximum acceleration occurs at extreme positions ($x = \pm A$, $a_{max} = \omega^2 A$).

2. Energy Transformations in SHM

In ideal frictionless harmonic systems, mechanical energy continuously shifts between kinetic energy ($K$) and potential energy ($U$), while total mechanical energy remains completely conserved over time.

$$E_{total} = K + U = \frac{1}{2}m\omega^2 A^2$$

  • Potential Energy ($U$): Varies quadratically with displacement according to $U(x) = \frac{1}{2} m \omega^2 x^2 = \frac{1}{2} k x^2$.
  • Kinetic Energy ($K$): Peak kinetic energy occurs at the mean position: $K(x) = \frac{1}{2} m \omega^2 (A^2 - x^2)$.
  • Equipartition Position: Kinetic and potential energies become equal ($K = U$) at displacement position $x = \pm \frac{A}{\sqrt{2}}$.

3. Spring Systems & Simple Pendulum Variations

Oscillation periods alter depending on system geometry, effective spring constants, and background gravitational fields.

Spring Combination Rules:

  • Series Spring Combination: $\frac{1}{k_{eq}} = \frac{1}{k_1} + \frac{1}{k_2} \implies T = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{m(k_1 + k_2)}{k_1 k_2}}$
  • Parallel Spring Combination: $k_{eq} = k_1 + k_2 \implies T = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{m}{k_1 + k_2}}$

Simple & Physical Pendulums:

For small angular displacements ($\theta \ll 1$), the simple pendulum time period depends solely on length and effective gravity:

$$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{L}{g_{eff}}}$$

Worked Numerical Example

Problem: A particle of mass $0.1\text{ kg}$ executes SHM with an amplitude of $0.05\text{ m}$ and a time period of $0.2\text{ s}$. Find the total mechanical energy of the particle.

Solution:

  1. Calculate angular velocity $\omega$: $\omega = \frac{2\pi}{T} = \frac{2\pi}{0.2} = 10\pi\text{ rad/s}$.
  2. Apply total energy formula: $E_{total} = \frac{1}{2} m \omega^2 A^2$.
  3. Substitute values: $E_{total} = \frac{1}{2} (0.1) (10\pi)^2 (0.05)^2 = 0.05 \times 100\pi^2 \times 0.0025 = 0.0125\pi^2\text{ J} \approx 0.123\text{ J}$.

JEE/NEET Key Takeaways

  • Potential energy and kinetic energy oscillate at twice the frequency ($2f$) of the displacement wave ($f$).
  • Cutting a spring of constant $k$ into $n$ equal pieces increases the spring constant of each individual segment to $n \cdot k$.

fields.title: Fluid Mechanics & Hydraulics: Pascal, Bernoulli, and Viscosity
fields.summary: A breakdown of hydrostatic pressure, continuity equations, Bernoulli's principle, surface tension, and Stokes' law
fields.content:
Fluid Mechanics examines the static and dynamic behavior of fluids, forming a critical segment of JEE and NEET physics. Understanding hydrostatics, stream dynamics, ideal fluid flow, and viscous forces is essential for mastering fluid calculations under varying pressure and flow conditions.

1. Hydrostatics & Pascal's Law

Fluid statics focuses on fluids at rest, where shear stresses are absent and pressure depends entirely on depth and fluid density. Pascal's Law states that any pressure change applied to an enclosed incompressible fluid is transmitted undiminished throughout the fluid and to the walls of its container.

$$P = P_0 + \rho g h$$

  • Gauge Pressure vs Absolute Pressure: Gauge pressure measures relative to ambient atmospheric pressure ($P_{gauge} = \rho g h$), whereas absolute pressure accounts for total atmospheric force ($P_{abs} = P_0 + \rho g h$).
  • Hydraulic Lift Principle: Force applied on a smaller piston of area $A_1$ creates an magnified output force on a larger piston of area $A_2$ through $F_2 = F_1 \left(\frac{A_2}{A_1}\right)$.
  • Archimedes' Principle & Buoyancy: An immersed object experiences an upward buoyant force equal to the weight of the fluid displaced ($F_b = \rho_{fluid} \cdot V_{submerged} \cdot g$).

2. Fluid Dynamics & Bernoulli's Equation

In steady, incompressible, and non-viscous streamline flow, mass conservation dictates the Equation of Continuity, ensuring that total mechanical energy remains conserved along any streamline.

$$A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2 \quad \text{and} \quad P + \frac{1}{2}\rho v^2 + \rho g h = \text{Constant}$$

Key Applications of Bernoulli's Principle:

  • Torricelli's Law of Efflux: The speed of efflux of a liquid leaking through a small hole at depth $h$ below the free surface equals $v = \sqrt{2gh}$.
  • Venturi Meter Flow Rate: Measures fluid velocity inside pipes by determining pressure difference across cross-sectional contractions using $\Delta P = \frac{1}{2}\rho (v_2^2 - v_1^2)$.

3. Viscosity, Stoke's Law & Surface Tension

Real fluids display internal friction between adjacent moving fluid layers, described by Newton's law of viscosity where shear stress is proportional to velocity gradient ($\eta$).

$$F_{viscous} = -\eta A \frac{dv}{dx} \quad \text{and} \quad F_{Stokes} = 6\pi \eta r v$$

  • Terminal Velocity: When gravitational force balances viscous drag and buoyant force, a spherical body falls through a fluid at a constant terminal velocity $v_t = \frac{2}{9} \frac{r^2 (\rho_{body} - \rho_{fluid}) g}{\eta}$.
  • Excess Pressure in Drops & Bubbles: Liquid drops experience an internal excess pressure of $\Delta P = \frac{2T}{R}$, whereas soap bubbles with two free surfaces experience $\Delta P = \frac{4T}{R}$.

Worked Numerical Example

Problem: Water flows horizontally through a pipe of varying cross-section. At point 1, the pressure is $2 \times 10^5\text{ Pa}$ and water velocity is $2\text{ m/s}$. Find the pressure at point 2 where the velocity increases to $4\text{ m/s}$ (Density of water $\rho = 1000\text{ kg/m}^3$).

Solution:

  1. Write Bernoulli's equation for horizontal flow ($h_1 = h_2$): $P_1 + \frac{1}{2}\rho v_1^2 = P_2 + \frac{1}{2}\rho v_2^2$.
  2. Rearrange for $P_2$: $P_2 = P_1 + \frac{1}{2}\rho (v_1^2 - v_2^2)$.
  3. Substitute values: $P_2 = 2 \times 10^5 + \frac{1}{2}(1000)(2^2 - 4^2) = 200,000 + 500(4 - 16) = 200,000 - 6,000 = 194,000\text{ Pa} = 1.94 \times 10^5\text{ Pa}$.

JEE/NEET Key Takeaways

  • Bernoulli's equation applies strictly along streamlines for non-viscous, incompressible, and irrotational steady fluid flows.
  • Terminal velocity scales directly with the square of the body's radius ($v_t \propto r^2$), making smaller mist droplets fall significantly slower than larger raindrops.

fields.title: Current Electricity: Circuit Solving Techniques & Measuring Instruments
fields.summary: Master Drift velocity, Kirchhoff's Laws, Wheatstone Bridge, Meter Bridge, and Galvanometer conversions
fields.content:
Current Electricity forms a cornerstone of competitive physics examinations, bridging fundamental charge dynamics with complex network analysis. Mastering nodal analysis, mesh loops, symmetry simplifications, and high-precision measuring tools like the Galvanometer, Potentiometer, and Meter Bridge is vital for solving advanced circuits quickly.

1. Fundamental Laws & Circuit Solving Techniques

Electric current represents net charge flow rate ($I = \frac{dQ}{dt} = n e A v_d$). Ohm's Law links current density to applied electric field ($\vec{J} = \sigma \vec{E}$). Complex networks require systematic application of Kirchhoff's Laws and network reduction principles.

$$\sum I_{in} = \sum I_{out} \quad \text{and} \quad \sum \Delta V = 0$$

  • Nodal Analysis Method: Select a reference node (ground at $0\text{ V}$), assign unknown potentials to remaining nodes, and apply Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL) using Ohm's law ($I = \frac{V_A - V_B}{R}$) to solve simultaneous equations.
  • Symmetry Simplifications: For symmetric resistive grids (cubes, ladders, bridges), identify equipotential nodes across axes of symmetry. Nodes at equal potential can be shorted together or disconnected without altering equivalent resistance.
  • Delta-Wye ($\Delta-\text{Y}$) Transformations: Converts a triangular delta network into a star wye network using $R_1 = \frac{R_{ab} R_{ca}}{R_{ab} + R_{bc} + R_{ca}}$.

2. Measuring Instruments & Conversion Principles

Precision electrical measurements rely on moving coil galvanometers adapted to measure prospective currents or potential drops across specific circuit elements.

$$S = \frac{I_g R_g}{I - I_g} \quad \text{and} \quad R_{series} = \frac{V}{I_g} - R_g$$

  • Ammeter Conversion: An ideal ammeter has zero internal resistance. A galvanometer of resistance $R_g$ and full-scale deflection current $I_g$ converts to an ammeter of range $I$ by shunting a small resistance $S$ in parallel.
  • Voltmeter Conversion: An ideal voltmeter has infinite resistance. Conversion to measure potential range $V$ requires connecting a large resistance $R_{series}$ in series with the galvanometer.
  • Potentiometer Null Method: Measures cell potential without drawing current at balance ($E \propto l$). Compares EMFs ($\frac{E_1}{E_2} = \frac{l_1}{l_2}$) and measures internal resistance ($r = R \left(\frac{l_1}{l_2} - 1\right)$).

Worked Numerical Example

Problem: A galvanometer has a resistance of $50\text{ }\Omega$ and gives full-scale deflection for a current of $2\text{ mA}$. Calculate the shunt resistance required to convert it into an ammeter capable of measuring currents up to $5\text{ A}$.

Solution:

  1. Identify parameters: $R_g = 50\text{ }\Omega$, $I_g = 2 \times 10^{-3}\text{ A}$, $I = 5\text{ A}$.
  2. Apply shunt resistance formula: $S = \frac{I_g R_g}{I - I_g}$.
  3. Substitute known values: $S = \frac{(2 \times 10^{-3})(50)}{5 - 0.002} = \frac{0.1}{4.998} \approx 0.02001\text{ }\Omega$.

JEE/NEET Key Takeaways

  • The Potentiometer is superior to a Voltmeter for measuring cell EMF because it draws zero current from the cell at the null point, preventing internal resistance potential drops.
  • Temperature dependence of resistance follows $R(T) = R_0 [1 + \alpha (T - T_0)]$, where conductors have positive $\alpha$ and semiconductors have negative $\alpha$.

fields.title: Semiconductor Electronics & Logic Gates Cheat Sheet
fields.summary: Energy bands, p-n junction diodes, rectifiers, Zener diode regulation, and Boolean logic gates
fields.content:
Semiconductor Physics forms the backbone of modern electronic devices, covering energy band structures, p-n junction diode characteristics, rectifiers, voltage regulators, and digital logic gates.

1. Energy Bands & Carrier Concentration

Solid materials are categorized based on their energy bandgap ($E_g$) between the filled valence band (VB) and empty conduction band (CB):

  • Conductors: VB and CB overlap ($E_g \approx 0\text{ eV}$).
  • Insulators: Large band gap ($E_g > 3\text{ eV}$).
  • Semiconductors: Small band gap ($E_g < 3\text{ eV}$; Silicon $E_g \approx 1.1\text{ eV}$, Germanium $E_g \approx 0.7\text{ eV}$).

Intrinsic vs Extrinsic Semiconductors:

In thermal equilibrium, intrinsic semiconductors obey mass-action law:

$$n_e \cdot n_h = n_i^2$$

  • n-type Semiconductor: Doped with pentavalent impurities (P, As, Sb). Electrons are majority carriers ($n_e \approx N_d \gg n_h$).
  • p-type Semiconductor: Doped with trivalent impurities (B, Al, In). Holes are majority carriers ($n_h \approx N_a \gg n_e$).

2. p-n Junction Diode & Rectifiers

Joining p-type and n-type semiconductors forms a depletion layer containing immobile ions, creating a barrier potential ($V_b \approx 0.7\text{V}$ for Si).

Biasing Modes:

  • Forward Bias: p-side connected to positive terminal. Depletion width decreases, allowing exponential diffusion current.
  • Reverse Bias: p-side connected to negative terminal. Depletion width increases, allowing only a small drift saturation current.

Diode Rectifiers:

  • Half-Wave Rectifier: Uses 1 diode. Maximum efficiency $\eta_{max} = 40.6\%$, Ripple factor $= 1.21$. Output frequency $= f_{in}$.
  • Full-Wave Rectifier (Center-Tapped/Bridge): Uses 2 or 4 diodes. Maximum efficiency $\eta_{max} = 81.2\%$, Ripple factor $= 0.48$. Output frequency $= 2f_{in}$.

Zener Diode as a Voltage Regulator:

A heavily doped p-n junction operated in reverse breakdown region keeps output voltage constant ($V_Z$) across changing load currents ($I_L$):

$$I_S = I_Z + I_L \implies I_S = \frac{V_{in} - V_Z}{R_S}$$

3. Digital Logic Gates Truth Table & Boolean Algebra

Logic gates process digital binary signals ($0$ and $1$).

Fundamental Gate Rules:

  • OR Gate ($Y = A + B$): Output is HIGH if at least one input is HIGH.
  • AND Gate ($Y = A \cdot B$): Output is HIGH only when all inputs are HIGH.
  • NOT Gate ($Y = \bar{A}$): Inverts the binary logic signal.
  • NAND Gate ($Y = \overline{A \cdot B}$): Universal gate. Output is LOW only when all inputs are HIGH.
  • NOR Gate ($Y = \overline{A + B}$): Universal gate. Output is HIGH only when all inputs are LOW.
  • XOR Gate ($Y = A \oplus B = A\bar{B} + \bar{A}B$): Output is HIGH when inputs differ.

De Morgan's Laws for Boolean Simplification:

$$\overline{A + B} = \bar{A} \cdot \bar{B} \quad \text{and} \quad \overline{A \cdot B} = \bar{A} + \bar{B}$$

Worked Numerical Example

Problem: In a Zener diode voltage regulator, $V_{in} = 15\text{ V}$, $V_Z = 9\text{ V}$, and series resistor $R_S = 100\,\Omega$. If load current $I_L = 20\text{ mA}$, calculate the current flowing through the Zener diode ($I_Z$).

Solution:

  1. Calculate total source current $I_S$: $I_S = \frac{V_{in} - V_Z}{R_S} = \frac{15 - 9}{100} = \frac{6}{100}\text{ A} = 60\text{ mA}$.
  2. Apply current node balance: $I_S = I_Z + I_L$.
  3. Solve for $I_Z$: $I_Z = I_S - I_L = 60\text{ mA} - 20\text{ mA} = 40\text{ mA}$.

JEE/NEET Key Takeaways

  • NAND and NOR gates are universal gates because any logic circuit can be constructed using only one of these gate types.
  • In intrinsic semiconductors, conductivity rises exponentially with temperature as covalent bonds break.

fields.title: Dual Nature of Radiation & Matter: De Broglie & Photoelectric Effect
fields.summary: Photon momentum, de Broglie wavelength relations, and photoelectric effect graphs
fields.content:
Modern Physics highlights quantum wave-particle duality, where light exhibits particle properties (photons) in the photoelectric effect and matter particles exhibit wave properties (de Broglie matter waves).

1. Photons & Photoelectric Effect Mechanics

Light consists of discrete energy packets called photons. The energy $E$ and momentum $p$ of a photon of frequency $\nu$ and wavelength $\lambda$ are:

$$E = h\nu = \frac{hc}{\lambda} \quad \text{and} \quad p = \frac{E}{c} = \frac{h}{\lambda}$$

Einstein's Photoelectric Equation:

When light strikes a clean metallic surface, a photon transfers its entire energy $h\nu$ to a single electron. Part of this energy overcomes the metal work function ($\Phi_0$), while the remainder becomes maximum kinetic energy ($K_{max}$):

$$h\nu = \Phi_0 + K_{max}$$

$$h\nu = h\nu_0 + e V_0 \implies e V_0 = hc\left(\frac{1}{\lambda} - \frac{1}{\lambda_0}\right)$$

  • Work Function ($\Phi_0 = h\nu_0$): Minimum energy needed to liberate an electron from the metal surface.
  • Threshold Frequency ($\nu_0$): Minimum light frequency below which zero photoelectric emission occurs, regardless of light intensity.
  • Stopping Potential ($V_0$): Retarding potential required to completely stop the fastest photoelectrons ($K_{max} = e V_0$).

Key Experimental Laws of Photoelectricity:

  • Photoelectric current is directly proportional to incident light intensity (for $\nu > \nu_0$).
  • Maximum kinetic energy $K_{max}$ and stopping potential $V_0$ depend linearly on frequency $\nu$, and are completely independent of light intensity.
  • The process is instantaneous (time lag $< 10^{-9}\text{ sec}$).

2. De Broglie Matter Wave Hypothesis

Louis de Broglie proposed that moving material particles possess a wave character. The de Broglie wavelength ($\lambda$) associated with a particle of mass $m$ and momentum $p$ is:

$$\lambda = \frac{h}{p} = \frac{h}{mv}$$

Alternative Expressions for De Broglie Wavelength:

  • In terms of Kinetic Energy ($K$): Since $p = \sqrt{2mK}$:

$$\lambda = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2mK}}$$

  • Accelerated Charged Particles ($q$ across potential difference $V$): Since $K = qV$:

$$\lambda = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2mqV}}$$

  • For Electrons specifically ($m_e, e$):

$$\lambda_e = \frac{12.27}{\sqrt{V}} \text{ \AA} = \sqrt{\frac{150}{V}} \text{ \AA}$$

  • Thermal Neutrons at temperature $T$: $\lambda_{thermal} = \frac{h}{\sqrt{3mk_B T}}$.

Worked Numerical Example

Problem: Calculate the stopping potential for electrons emitted from a metal surface of work function $2.0\text{ eV}$ when illuminated by photons of energy $4.5\text{ eV}$.

Solution:

  1. Apply Einstein's equation: $h\nu = \Phi_0 + K_{max}$.
  2. Calculate $K_{max}$: $K_{max} = 4.5\text{ eV} - 2.0\text{ eV} = 2.5\text{ eV}$.
  3. Since $K_{max} = e V_0$, substitute $2.5\text{ eV} = e V_0$.
  4. The stopping potential is $V_0 = 2.5\text{ Volts}$.

JEE/NEET Exam Strategy Notes

  • The slope of a $V_0$ versus $\nu$ graph yields the ratio $\frac{h}{e}$, which is a universal physical constant.
  • Photons carry zero rest mass and are electrically neutral; they are not deflected by magnetic or electric fields.

fields.title: Center of Mass & Momentum Conservation: Problem-Solving Guide
fields.summary: Position vectors of COM, mass removal problems, variable mass systems, and impulse equations
fields.content:
Center of mass (COM) and linear momentum conservation form the core foundation for solving complex multi-particle systems, variable-mass problems, and collisions in classical mechanics.

1. Position and Motion of Center of Mass

The Center of Mass is a uniquely defined point where the total mass of a system can be treated as concentrated for translational motion analysis under external forces.

Discrete Particle Systems:

$$\vec{r}_{cm} = \frac{m_1\vec{r}_1 + m_2\vec{r}_2 + \dots + m_n\vec{r}_n}{m_1 + m_2 + \dots + m_n} = \frac{\sum m_i \vec{r}_i}{M_{total}}$$

Continuous Mass Distributions:

$$\vec{r}_{cm} = \frac{1}{M} \int \vec{r} \, dm$$

Velocity and Acceleration of Center of Mass:

$$\vec{v}_{cm} = \frac{\sum m_i \vec{v}_i}{M_{total}} \quad \text{and} \quad \vec{a}_{cm} = \frac{\sum m_i \vec{a}_i}{M_{total}} = \frac{\vec{F}_{ext, net}}{M_{total}}$$

Key Note: Internal forces between particles cancel out in pairs by Newton's Third Law and cannot alter the motion of the center of mass.

2. Standard Center of Mass Locations

  • Uniform Thin Rod (Length L): At mid-point ($x_{cm} = L/2$).
  • Uniform Semi-Circular Ring (Radius R): $y_{cm} = \frac{2R}{\pi}$ above diameter.
  • Uniform Semi-Circular Disc (Radius R): $y_{cm} = \frac{4R}{3\pi}$ above diameter.
  • Hollow Hemisphere (Radius R): $y_{cm} = \frac{R}{2}$ above base center.
  • Solid Hemisphere (Radius R): $y_{cm} = \frac{3R}{8}$ above base center.
  • Solid Cone (Height h): $y_{cm} = \frac{h}{4}$ above base center.

3. Conservation of Linear Momentum

According to Newton's Second Law, $\vec{F}_{ext, net} = \frac{d\vec{P}_{total}}{dt}$. If the net external force on a system is zero ($\vec{F}_{ext} = 0$), the total linear momentum remains conserved:

$$\vec{P}_{initial} = \vec{P}_{final} \implies M \vec{v}_{cm} = \text{Constant}$$

4. Collisions in One and Two Dimensions

Collisions involve brief, strong interactions between bodies. Total linear momentum is conserved in all isolated collisions, but mechanical energy conservation depends on collision elasticity.

Coefficient of Restitution ($e$):

The coefficient of restitution quantifies collision elasticity along the line of impact:

$$e = \frac{\text{Velocity of Separation}}{\text{Velocity of Approach}} = \frac{v_2 - v_1}{u_1 - u_2}$$

  • Perfectly Elastic Collision ($e = 1$): Kinetic energy is completely conserved ($\Delta K = 0$).
  • Inelastic Collision ($0 < e < 1$): Kinetic energy is partially lost to heat and deformation.
  • Completely Inelastic Collision ($e = 0$): Colliding bodies stick together and move with common velocity $v_{common} = \frac{m_1 u_1 + m_2 u_2}{m_1 + m_2}$.

Formula for Final Velocities in 1D Elastic Collisions ($e = 1$):

$$v_1 = \left(\frac{m_1 - m_2}{m_1 + m_2}\right)u_1 + \left(\frac{2m_2}{m_1 + m_2}\right)u_2$$

$$v_2 = \left(\frac{2m_1}{m_1 + m_2}\right)u_1 + \left(\frac{m_2 - m_1}{m_1 + m_2}\right)u_2$$

Worked Numerical Example

Problem: A body of mass $2\text{ kg}$ moving at $6\text{ m/s}$ collides head-on elastically ($e=1$) with a stationary body of mass $4\text{ kg}$. Find the final velocity of the $4\text{ kg}$ body.

Solution:

  1. Given $m_1 = 2\text{ kg}$, $u_1 = 6\text{ m/s}$, $m_2 = 4\text{ kg}$, $u_2 = 0\text{ m/s}$.
  2. Apply formula for $v_2$: $v_2 = \left(\frac{2m_1}{m_1 + m_2}\right)u_1 + 0$.
  3. Substitute values: $v_2 = \left(\frac{2 \times 2}{2 + 4}\right) \times 6 = \left(\frac{4}{6}\right) \times 6 = 4\text{ m/s}$.

JEE/NEET Key Takeaways

  • If two identical masses ($m_1 = m_2$) undergo a 1D elastic collision, they completely exchange their velocities upon impact.
  • When a projectile explodes in mid-air, the internal explosive forces do not alter the parabolic path of the center of mass.

fields.title: Nuclear Physics & Radioactivity: Binding Energy and Decay Laws
fields.summary: Mass defect, binding energy per nucleon, radioactive decay law, half-life, and nuclear reactions
fields.content:
Nuclear Physics explores atomic nuclear structure, binding energy dynamics, nuclear forces, and radioactive decay processes. Master mass deficit calculations, radioactive decay rates, half-life mechanics, and Q-value calculations for competitive physics exams.

1. Nuclear Size, Density & Mass Defect

The atomic nucleus contains positive protons and neutral neutrons (collectively called nucleons). Nuclear radius scales with atomic mass number ($A$).

Nuclear Radius & Density Equations:

$$R = R_0 A^{1/3} \quad (R_0 \approx 1.2 \times 10^{-15}\text{ m} = 1.2\text{ fm})$$

Nuclear density is approximately independent of mass number $A$ and remains nearly constant across all elements at $\rho_{nuclear} \approx 2.3 \times 10^{17}\text{ kg/m}^3$.

Mass Defect ($\Delta m$) & Binding Energy ($BE$):

The rest mass of a stable nucleus is always less than the sum of rest masses of its constituent free nucleons. This difference is the mass defect:

$$\Delta m = [Z \cdot m_p + (A - Z) \cdot m_n] - m_{nucleus}$$

Applying Einstein's mass-energy equivalence ($E = mc^2$), total Binding Energy is:

$$BE = \Delta m \times 931.5\text{ MeV} \quad (\text{when } \Delta m \text{ is in amu})$$

2. Binding Energy per Nucleon Curve

The Binding Energy per Nucleon ($BE/A$) determines overall nuclear stability:

  • $BE/A$ is low for very light nuclei ($A < 20$), rises sharply, and reaches a broad maximum of $\approx 8.8\text{ MeV/nucleon}$ near Iron ($^{56}\text{Fe}$).
  • For heavy nuclei ($A > 100$), $BE/A$ gradually decreases to $\approx 7.6\text{ MeV/nucleon}$ for Uranium ($^{238}\text{U}$).
  • Nuclear Fusion: Light nuclei combine to move higher up the $BE/A$ curve, releasing energy.
  • Nuclear Fission: Heavy nuclei split into medium-mass fragments to gain $BE/A$ stability, releasing energy.

3. Laws of Radioactive Decay

Radioactivity is a spontaneous nuclear transformation unaffected by external temperature or pressure. The rate of decay (Activity $A$) is proportional to the number of undecayed nuclei $N(t)$ present.

Decay Formulas:

$$\frac{dN}{dt} = -\lambda N \implies N(t) = N_0 e^{-\lambda t}$$

Activity: $A(t) = -\frac{dN}{dt} = \lambda N(t) = A_0 e^{-\lambda t}$ (SI Unit: $1\text{ Becquerel (Bq)} = 1\text{ decay/sec}$).

Half-Life ($T_{1/2}$) and Mean Life ($\tau$):

  • Half-Life ($T_{1/2}$): Time taken for half the sample nuclei to decay:

$$T_{1/2} = \frac{\ln(2)}{\lambda} \approx \frac{0.693}{\lambda}$$

  • Mean Life ($\tau$): Average lifespan of a radioactive nucleus:

$$\tau = \frac{1}{\lambda} = \frac{T_{1/2}}{0.693} \approx 1.44 \cdot T_{1/2}$$

  • Fraction remaining after $n$ half-lives: $N = N_0 \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^n$ where $n = \frac{t}{T_{1/2}}$.

4. Radioactivity Modes: $\alpha$, $\beta$, and $\gamma$ Decays

  • Alpha Decay ($\alpha$): Nucleus emits a Helium nucleus ($^{4}_{2}\text{He}$). Mass decreases by 4, atomic number decreases by 2: $^{Z}_{A}\text{X} \rightarrow ^{Z-2}_{A-4}\text{Y} + ^{4}_{2}\text{He} + Q$.
  • Beta-Minus Decay ($\beta^-$): A neutron converts into a proton, emitting an electron and antineutrino ($\bar{\nu}$): $n \rightarrow p + e^- + \bar{\nu}$. Atomic number increases by 1.
  • Beta-Plus Decay ($\beta^+$): A proton converts into a neutron, emitting a positron ($e^+$) and neutrino ($\nu$): $p \rightarrow n + e^+ + \nu$. Atomic number decreases by 1.
  • Gamma Decay ($\gamma$): Excited nucleus drops to a lower energy state by emitting a high-energy photon without changing $Z$ or $A$.

Worked Numerical Example

Problem: A radioactive sample has a half-life of 20 minutes. How long will it take for the sample's activity to drop to $1/16$th of its initial value?

Solution:

  1. Use fraction remaining relation: $\frac{A}{A_0} = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^n = \frac{1}{16}$.
  2. Since $(1/2)^4 = 1/16$, the number of half-lives $n = 4$.
  3. Total time required: $t = n \times T_{1/2} = 4 \times 20\text{ minutes} = 80\text{ minutes}$.

JEE/NEET Quick Memory Rules

  • Nuclear forces are short-range ($\approx 1\text{ fm}$), charge-independent, and non-central forces that saturate quickly.
  • $1\text{ Curie (Ci)} = 3.7 \times 10^{10}\text{ decays/sec}$.

fields.title: Electromagnetic Waves: Maxwell Equations and Spectrum Summary
fields.summary: Displacement current, Maxwell's equations, EM wave intensity, and electromagnetic spectrum properties
fields.content:
Electromagnetic (EM) waves are coupled, time-varying electric and magnetic fields propagating through space at the speed of light. This guide covers Maxwell's fundamental equations, displacement current, wave energy density, the Poynting vector, and the complete EM spectrum for JEE and NEET Physics.

1. Maxwell's Equations & Displacement Current

James Clerk Maxwell unified electricity and magnetism into four fundamental equations and corrected Ampere's Law to account for time-varying electric fields by introducing displacement current.

Maxwell's Four Fundamental Equations:

  • Gauss' Law for Electricity: $\oint \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{A} = \frac{Q_{enclosed}}{\varepsilon_0}$ (Electric charges produce electric fields).
  • Gauss' Law for Magnetism: $\oint \vec{B} \cdot d\vec{A} = 0$ (Magnetic monopoles do not exist).
  • Faraday's Law of Induction: $\oint \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{l} = -\frac{d\Phi_B}{dt}$ (Changing magnetic flux induces an electric field).
  • Ampere-Maxwell Law: $\oint \vec{B} \cdot d\vec{l} = \mu_0 I_c + \mu_0 \varepsilon_0 \frac{d\Phi_E}{dt}$ (Conduction current and changing electric flux generate magnetic fields).

Displacement Current ($I_d$):

Displacement current arises in regions where the electric flux changes with time, such as between the plates of a charging capacitor:

$$I_d = \varepsilon_0 \frac{d\Phi_E}{dt}$$

2. Properties of Electromagnetic Waves

EM waves are transverse in nature where electric field $\vec{E}$, magnetic field $\vec{B}$, and propagation direction $\vec{k}$ are mutually perpendicular ($\vec{E} \times \vec{B}$ points in the wave direction).

Core Mathematical Wave Relations:

  • Speed of Light in Vacuum ($c$):

$$c = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0 \varepsilon_0}} = \frac{E_0}{B_0} \approx 3 \times 10^8 \text{ m/s}$$

  • Speed in a Material Medium ($v$): $v = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu \varepsilon}} = \frac{c}{\sqrt{\mu_r \varepsilon_r}} = \frac{c}{n}$ (where $n$ is the refractive index).
  • Energy Density ($u$): Total average energy density is shared equally between electric and magnetic fields:

$$u_{avg} = u_E + u_B = \frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 E_{rms}^2 + \frac{B_{rms}^2}{2\mu_0} = \frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 E_0^2$$

Poynting Vector & Wave Intensity:

The Poynting vector $\vec{S}$ represents energy flux (power per unit area) transported by an EM wave:

$$\vec{S} = \frac{1}{\mu_0} (\vec{E} \times \vec{B})$$

Average Intensity ($I$): $I = S_{avg} = c \cdot u_{avg} = \frac{1}{2} c \varepsilon_0 E_0^2$.

3. The Electromagnetic Spectrum Summary

Ordered by increasing frequency ($\nu$) and decreasing wavelength ($\lambda$):

  • Radio Waves ($\lambda > 0.1\text{ m}$): Produced by accelerated charges in conducting wires. Used in broad communication.
  • Microwaves ($1\text{ mm} - 0.1\text{ m}$): Produced by special vacuum tubes (klystrons/magnetrons). Used in radar and cooking.
  • Infrared Rays ($700\text{ nm} - 1\text{ mm}$): Produced by hot bodies and molecules. Used in thermal imaging and night vision.
  • Visible Light ($400\text{ nm} - 700\text{ nm}$): Emitted by atomic electron transitions. Detected by human eyes.
  • Ultraviolet Rays ($1\text{ nm} - 400\text{ nm}$): Emitted by inner shell electron transitions and the sun. Used in sterilization.
  • X-Rays ($10^{-3}\text{ nm} - 1\text{ nm}$): Produced by bombarding heavy metal targets with high-energy electrons. Used in medical imaging.
  • Gamma Rays ($\lambda < 10^{-3}\text{ nm}$): Produced in nuclear reactions and radioactive decay. Used in cancer radiotherapy.

Worked Numerical Example

Problem: In a plane EM wave, the peak electric field amplitude is $E_0 = 150\text{ N/C}$. Calculate the amplitude of the magnetic field $B_0$ and the average energy density $u_{avg}$.

Solution:

  1. Calculate $B_0$: $B_0 = \frac{E_0}{c} = \frac{150}{3 \times 10^8} = 5 \times 10^{-7}\text{ Tesla}$.
  2. Calculate $u_{avg}$: $u_{avg} = \frac{1}{2} \varepsilon_0 E_0^2 = \frac{1}{2} \times (8.85 \times 10^{-12}) \times (150)^2$.
  3. $u_{avg} = 0.5 \times 8.85 \times 10^{-12} \times 22500 = 9.95 \times 10^{-8}\text{ J/m}^3$.

JEE/NEET Key Takeaways

  • Radiation pressure on a completely absorbing surface is P = $\frac{I}{c}$; on a completely reflecting surface, it doubles to P = $\frac{2I}{c}$.
  • Displacement current flows whenever electric field intensity varies inside a dielectric or vacuum gap.

fields.title: Units, Dimensions & Error Analysis: High-Scoring Basics
fields.summary: Dimensional formulas of fundamental constants, vernier calipers, screw gauge, and error propagation rules
fields.content:
Units, Dimensions, and Error Analysis constitute one of the most reliable scoring chapters in both JEE Main and NEET Physics. Questions from this topic are straightforward, provided you understand dimensional formulas, significant figures, propagation of experimental errors, and vernier caliper / screw gauge reading mechanisms.

1. Fundamental Units & Dimensional Analysis

All physical quantities in mechanics, thermodynamics, and electromagnetism can be expressed in terms of seven fundamental SI base units: Mass [M], Length [L], Time [T], Electric Current [I or A], Absolute Temperature [K or $\theta$], Amount of Substance [mol], and Luminous Intensity [cd].

Dimensional Formulas for Frequently Tested Quantities:

  • Force & Weight: [$M^1$ $L^1$ $T^{-2}$]
  • Work, Energy & Torque: [$M^1$ $L^2$ $T^{-2}$]
  • Pressure, Stress & Young's Modulus: [$M^1$ $L^{-1}$ $T^{-2}$]
  • Plancks Constant (h): [$M^1$ $L^2$ $T^{-1}$]
  • Universal Gravitational Constant (G): [$M^{-1}$ $L^3$ $T^{-2}$]
  • Coefficient of Viscosity ($\eta$): [$M^1$ $L^{-1}$ $T^{-1}$]
  • Permittivity of Free Space ($\epsilon_₀$): [$M^{-1}$ $L^{-3}$ $T^4$ $A^2$]
  • Permeability of Free Space ($\mu_₀$): [$M^1$ $L^1$ $T^{-2}$ $A^{-2}$]

Principle of Homogeneity of Dimensions: In any physically valid equation, the dimensions of all terms separated by addition (+), subtraction (-), or equality (=) signs must be identical.

2. Propagation of Errors

When physical quantities are calculated from measured experimental values containing absolute errors ($\Delta$ x, $\Delta$ y), errors propagate based on mathematical operation rules.

Error Combination Equations:

1. Addition and Subtraction (Z = A + B or Z = A - B):

$\Delta$ Z = $\Delta$ A + $\Delta$ B $\quad$ $\text{(Absolute errors always add up)}$

2. Multiplication and Division (Z = A $\cdot$ B or Z = $\frac{A}{B}$):

$\frac{\Delta Z}{Z}$ = $\frac{\Delta A}{A}$ + $\frac{\Delta B}{B}$ $\quad$ $\text{(Relative errors add up)}$

3. Power Rule Exponents (Z = $\frac{A^p B^q}{C^r}$):

For a physical relationship governed by exponents, maximum fractional error is calculated as:

$\frac{\Delta Z}{Z}$ = p $\left(\frac{\Delta A}{A}\right)$ + q $\left(\frac{\Delta B}{B}\right)$ + r $\left(\frac{\Delta C}{C}\right)$

Percentage error in Z is obtained by multiplying fractional error by 100$\%$.

3. Measuring Instruments: Vernier Caliper & Screw Gauge

Vernier Caliper Mechanics:

Least Count (LC) represents the minimum length measurement possible with the instrument.

$\text{Least Count (LC)}$ = 1 $\text{ MSD}$ - 1 $\text{ VSD}$ = $\left(1 - \frac{N-1}{N}\right)$ $\text{ MSD}$ = $\frac{1 \text{ MSD}}{N}$

where MSD = Main Scale Division, VSD = Vernier Scale Division, N = total vernier scale divisions matching (N-1) main scale divisions.

$\text{Total Reading}$ = $\text{Main Scale Reading (MSR)}$ + $(\text{Vernier Scale Coincidence}$ $\times$ $\text{LC})$ - $\text{Zero Error}$

Screw Gauge / Micrometer Mechanics:

  • Pitch: Distance moved by the spindle on the main scale per full rotation of the thimble head.
  • Least Count (LC):

$\text{LC}$ = $\frac{\text{Pitch}}{\text{Total Circular Scale Divisions}}$

Worked Numerical Example

Problem: The physical density of a solid sphere is determined using formula $\rho$ = $\frac{M}{\frac{4}{3} \pi R^3}$. If the percentage error in measuring Mass M is 2$\%$ and Radius R is 1.5$\%$, calculate the maximum percentage error in density.

Solution:

  1. Write error expression: $\frac{\Delta\rho}{\rho}$ $\times$ 100 = $\left(\frac{\Delta M}{M} + 3\frac{\Delta R}{R}\right)$ $\times$ 100
  2. Substitute measured percentage errors: $\text{% Error}$ = 2$\%$ + 3(1.5$\%$)
  3. Simplify arithmetic: $\text{% Error}$ = 2$\%$ + 4.5$\%$ = 6.5$\%$

Conclusion: The total maximum percentage error in density is 6.5$\%$.

JEE/NEET High-Yield Tips

  • Constant numeric factors (like 4, 1/2, or $\pi$) carry zero dimensional error and do not contribute to error calculations.
  • Arguments of trigonometric, exponential, and logarithmic functions must always be dimensionless quantities.

fields.title: Thermal Properties of Matter & Heat Transfer: Complete Summary
fields.summary: Thermal expansion, calorimetry, conduction, Stefan-Boltzmann law, and Wien's displacement law
fields.content:
Thermal Physics forms a fundamental portion of competitive entrance exams, connecting temperature-induced dimensional expansions with calorimetry, phase change thermodynamics, and thermal heat transfer mechanisms. This review guide covers thermal expansion coefficients, specific heat capacities, heat transfer conduction laws, Stefan-Boltzmann radiation, and Wien's displacement law.

1. Thermal Expansion in Solids and Liquids

When temperature rises by $\Delta$ T, solids expand linearly, superficially (area), and volumetrically (cubical). For isotropic materials, these expansion coefficients maintain fixed proportional ratios.

Expansion Equations:

  • Linear Expansion: L = $L_0$ (1 + $\alpha$ $\Delta$ T) → $\Delta$ L = $L_0$ $\alpha$ $\Delta$ T
  • Area Expansion: A = $A_0$ (1 + $\beta$ $\Delta$ T) → $\Delta$ A = $A_0$ $\beta$ $\Delta$ T
  • Volume Expansion: V = $V_0$ (1 + $\gamma$ $\Delta$ T) → $\Delta$ V = $V_0$ $\gamma$ $\Delta$ T

Proportional Relationship for Isotropic Solids:

$\alpha$ : $\beta$ : $\gamma$ = 1 : 2 : 3 implies $\beta$ = 2$\alpha$ $\quad$ $\text{and}$ $\quad$ $\gamma$ = 3$\alpha$

Thermal Stress in Stopped Rods:

If a rigid rod clamped between two unyielding walls undergoes a temperature decrease or increase $\Delta$ T, thermal stress develops in the material:

$\text{Thermal Stress}$ = $\frac{F}{A}$ = Y $\cdot$ $\alpha$ $\cdot$ $\Delta$ T

where Y is Young's modulus of elasticity of the material.

2. Calorimetry & Latent Heat

Calorimetry relies on the principle of thermal energy conservation in an isolated system: Heat Lost = Heat Gained.

Fundamental Calorimetry Formulas:

  • Sensible Heat Transfer (Temperature Change): Q = m $\cdot$ c $\cdot$ $\Delta$ T = C $\cdot$ $\Delta$ T (where c is specific heat capacity, C is total heat capacity).
  • Latent Heat Transfer (Phase Change at Constant T): Q = m $\cdot$ L (where L is latent heat of fusion or vaporization).
  • Molar Heat Capacity: $C_m$ = $\frac{1}{n}$ $\frac{dQ}{dT}$

3. Conduction Heat Transfer & Thermal Resistance

Conduction represents heat transfer through direct molecular collisions across a temperature gradient without actual bulk movement of matter. According to Fourier's Law of Thermal Conduction, heat current (H = $\frac{dQ}{dt}$) flowing across a slab of cross-sectional area A and length L with temperature difference (T₁ - T₂) is:

H = $\frac{dQ}{dt}$ = $\frac{K \cdot A \cdot (T_1 - T_2)}{L}$

Thermal Resistance Analogy (Ohm's Law Analogy):

Comparing thermal conduction to electrical conduction (I = $\Delta$ V / R), thermal resistance ($R_th$) is defined as:

$R_{th}$ = $\frac{L}{K \cdot A}$

  • Slabs in Series: $R_{eq}$ = $R_1$ + $R_2$ = $\frac{L_1}{K_1 A}$ + $\frac{L_2}{K_2 A}$
  • Slabs in Parallel: $\frac{1}{R_{eq}}$ = $\frac{1}{R_1}$ + $\frac{1}{R_2}$ = $\frac{K_1 A_1}{L}$ + $\frac{K_2 A_2}{L}$

4. Radiation Laws: Stefan-Boltzmann & Wien's Displacement

Thermal radiation involves heat transfer via electromagnetic waves without requiring a intervening material medium.

Stefan-Boltzmann Law:

The total radiant energy emitted per unit surface area per unit time by a blackbody is directly proportional to the fourth power of its absolute temperature (T in Kelvin):

E = $\sigma$ $T^{4}$

For a non-blackbody object of emissivity e and surface area A at temperature T in surroundings at temperature T₀, net power lost is:

$P_{net}$ = e $\sigma$ A ($T^{4} - T_0^{4}$)

Wien's Displacement Law:

The wavelength ($\lambda$_m) corresponding to maximum spectral emissive power of a blackbody is inversely proportional to its absolute temperature T:

$\lambda_m$ $\cdot$ T = b $\approx$ 2.898 $\times$ $10^{-3}$ , $\text{m}$ $\cdot$ $\text{K}$

Worked Numerical Example

Problem: A blackbody at temperature 3000 K emits radiation with peak intensity at wavelength $\lambda$_m = 1000 nm. Calculate the temperature of a star whose emission peak occurs at 500 nm.

Solution:

  1. Apply Wien's Law: $\lambda_1$ $\cdot$ $T_1$ = $\lambda_2$ $\cdot$ $T_2$
  2. Substitute values: 1000 $\text{ nm}$ $\times$ 3000 $\text{ K}$ = 500 $\text{ nm}$ $\times$ $T_2$
  3. Solve for T₂: $T_2$ = $\frac{1000 \times 3000}{500}$ = 6000 $\text{ K}$

Conclusion: The star's surface temperature is 6000 K.

JEE/NEET Quick Memory Rules

  • Water exhibits anomalous expansion between 0°C and 4°C, where its density is maximum at 4°C.
  • In Newton's Law of Cooling ($\frac{dT}{dt}$ = -k(T - $T_0$)), temperatures can be used in Celsius because it depends on temperature differences ($\Delta$ T).

fields.title: Rigid Body Dynamics: Rolling Without Slipping & Energy Methods
fields.summary: A complete guide to instant center of rotation, pure rolling conditions on inclined planes, and angular impulse
fields.content:
Rigid Body Dynamics is one of the most challenging and high-weightage chapters in mechanics for JEE Main, JEE Advanced, and NEET. A rigid body undergoing combined translational and rotational motion requires a firm grasp of moment of inertia tensor simplification, torque-angular acceleration relationships, pure rolling constraints, and energy conservation equations.

1. Moment of Inertia (I) & Fundamental Theorems

The moment of inertia represents a body's resistance to rotational acceleration about a specific axis. It depends on the distribution of mass relative to that axis: I = $\sum$ $m_i$ $(r_i)^{2}$ = $\int$ r² dm.

Core Theorems:

  • Parallel Axis Theorem: Applies to any shape body. The moment of inertia about an axis parallel to a center-of-mass axis separated by distance 'd' is given by:

I = $I_{cm}$ + $Md^{2}$

  • Perpendicular Axis Theorem: Applies strictly to planar (2D) thin lamina in the xy-plane:

$I_z$ = $I_x$ + $I_y$

Standard Moments of Inertia Reference Table:

  • Thin Circular Ring (Radius R): $I_{cm}$ = MR²
  • Uniform Circular Disc (Radius R): $I_{cm}$ = $\frac{1}{2}$MR²
  • Solid Cylinder (Radius R): $I_{cm}$ = $\frac{1}{2}$MR²
  • Solid Sphere (Radius R): $I_{cm}$ = $\frac{2}{5}$MR²
  • Hollow Thin Sphere (Radius R): $I_{cm}$ = $\frac{2}{3}$MR²
  • Thin Rod (Length L, about center): $I_{cm}$ = $\frac{1}{12}$ML²

2. Pure Rolling Motion (Rolling Without Slipping)

Pure rolling represents a combined motion where a rigid body undergoes simultaneous translation of its center of mass ($v_cm$) and rotation about its center of mass ($\omega$). The condition for pure rolling on a stationary surface is that the point of contact must be instantaneously at rest relative to the surface.

Pure Rolling Constraint Condition:

$v_{cm}$ = R$\omega$ $\quad$ $\text{and}$ $\quad$ $a_{cm}$ = R$\alpha$

Velocity of Any Arbitrary Point on a Rolling Body:

For a point located at angle θ relative to the lowest contact point on a circular body of radius R moving at speed $v_cm$, the net magnitude of velocity is:

$v_{net}$ = 2$v_{cm}$ sin$\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)$

  • Lowest Point (Contact Point, $\theta$ = 0°): v = 0
  • Center Point ($\theta$ = 90° relative to radius line): v = $v_{cm}$
  • Topmost Point ($\theta$ = 180°): v = 2$v_{cm}$

3. Acceleration of a Body Rolling Down an Inclined Plane

When a symmetric body (radius R, radius of gyration K) rolls down a rough inclined plane of inclination angle θ without slipping under gravity, friction acts up the incline to provide the required torque.

Linear Acceleration Formula:

a = $\frac{g \times sin(\theta)}{1 + \frac{K^{2}}{R^{2}}}$

Minimum Friction Coefficient ($\mu$) required for pure rolling:

$\mu_{min}$ = $\frac{tan(\theta)}{1 + \frac{R^{2}}{K^{2}}}$

4. Total Kinetic Energy in Combined Motion

The total kinetic energy ($K_{total}$) of a rolling rigid body is the sum of its translational kinetic energy of the center of mass and its rotational kinetic energy about the center of mass:

$K_{total}$ = $K_{trans}$ + $K_{rot}$ = $\frac{1}{2}$M $v_{cm}^{2}$ + $\frac{1}{2}$ $I_{cm}$ $\omega^{2}$

Using $v_{cm}$ = R$\omega$ and radius of gyration $I_{cm}$ = MK², this condenses to:

$K_{total}$ = $\frac{1}{2}$M $v_{cm}^{2}$ $\left(1 + \frac{K^{2}}{R^{2}}\right)$

Worked Numerical Example

Problem: A solid sphere ($\frac{K²}{R²}$ = $\frac{2}{5}$) and a uniform disc ($\frac{K²}{R²}$ = $\frac{1}{2}$) are released simultaneously from rest at the top of an inclined plane. Which object reaches the bottom first?

Solution:

  1. Acceleration formula: a = $\frac{g \times sin(\theta)}{1 + \frac{K²}{R²}}$
  2. For Solid Sphere: $a_{sphere}$ = $\frac{g \times sin(\theta)}{1 + \frac{2}{5}}$ = $\frac{5}{7}$ g $\times$ sin($\theta$) $\approx$ 0.714 ,g \times sin($\theta$)
  3. For Disc: $a_{disc}$ = $\frac{g \times sin(\theta)}{1 + \frac{1}{2}}$ = $\frac{2}{3}$ g $\times$ sin($\theta$) $\approx$ 0.667 ,g $\times$ sin($\theta$)
  4. Since $a_{sphere}$ > $a_{disc}$, the solid sphere experiences higher linear acceleration down the plane.

Conclusion: The solid sphere reaches the bottom first because less fraction of its initial potential energy converts into rotational kinetic energy compared to the disc.

JEE/NEET Exam Strategy Notes

  • Friction force in pure rolling does zero net work on the system because the instantaneous point of contact has zero displacement relative to the surface.
  • Never apply the perpendicular axis theorem to 3D solid shapes (like spheres, cones, or cylinders); it is strictly limited to flat planar sheets.

fields.title: Wave Optics: Wavefronts, Diffraction, & Malus' Law
fields.summary: Single slit diffraction minima/maxima, Brewster's angle, Malus' law, and resolving power of optical instruments
fields.content:
Wave optics deals with the wave nature of light, explaining phenomena like interference, diffraction, and polarization that ray optics cannot account for. Mastering Huygens' principle, Young's Double Slit Experiment (YDSE), single-slit diffraction, and polarization laws is essential for securing top ranks in JEE Main, JEE Advanced, and NEET Physics.

1. Huygens' Principle & Wavefronts

A wavefront is defined as the locus of all points in a medium having the same phase of oscillation. According to Huygens' Principle, every point on a primary wavefront acts as a secondary source of spherical wavelets that spread out in all directions with the speed of light in that medium.

  • Spherical Wavefront: Produced by a point source of light at a finite distance. Intensity varies inversely as the square of distance (I $\propto$ $\frac{1}{r^{2}}$).
  • Cylindrical Wavefront: Produced by a linear source (like a slit). Intensity varies inversely as distance (I $\propto$ $\frac{1}{r}$).
  • Plane Wavefront: Produced by a source located at infinity. Intensity remains constant with distance.

2. Interference & Young's Double Slit Experiment (YDSE)

Interference is the redistribution of light energy due to the superposition of two coherent light waves having constant phase difference ($\phi$).

Resultant Intensity Equation:

I = $I_1$ + $I_2$ + 2$\sqrt{I_1 \times I_2}$ cos($\phi$)

If two identical sources are used where I₁ = I₂ = I₀, the formula simplifies to:

I = 4$I_0$ $cos^{2}$ $\left(\frac{\phi}{2}\right)$

Fringe Width & Path Difference Formulas:

  • Path Difference ($\Delta$ x): $\Delta$ x = d $\cdot$ sin($\theta$) $\approx$ $\frac{yd}{D}$
  • Constructive Interference (Bright Fringes): $\Delta$ x = n$\lambda$ → Position $y_n$ = $\frac{n\lambda D}{d}$ (where n = 0, 1, 2...)
  • Destructive Interference (Dark Fringes): $\Delta$ x = (2n - 1) $\frac{\lambda}{2}$ → Position $y_n$ = $\frac{(2n - 1)\lambda D}{2d}$
  • Fringe Width ($\beta$): The distance between two consecutive bright or dark fringes:

$\beta$ = $\frac{\lambda D}{d}$

3. Single Slit Diffraction

Diffraction is the bending of light waves around the edges of an obstacle or narrow aperture into the geometrical shadow region.

Minima and Maxima Conditions for Slit Width (a):

  • Condition for Minima (Dark Fringes): a $\cdot$ sin($\theta$) = n$\lambda$ (where n = 1, 2, 3...)
  • Condition for Secondary Maxima (Bright Fringes): a $\cdot$ sin($\theta$) = (2n + 1)$\frac{\lambda}{2}$
  • Angular Width of Central Maximum: 2$\theta_0$ = $\frac{2\lambda}{a}$
  • Linear Width of Central Maximum (2y₀):

2$y_0$ = $\frac{2\lambda D}{a}$

4. Polarization of Light & Malus' Law

Light is a transverse electromagnetic wave where electric field vectors vibrate perpendicular to the direction of propagation. Unpolarized light consists of electric vectors vibrating in all possible perpendicular planes.

Brewster's Law (Polarization by Reflection):

When unpolarized light is incident at Brewster's angle ($\theta_p$) on a transparent medium, the reflected ray is completely plane-polarized perpendicular to the plane of incidence, and the reflected and refracted rays are mutually perpendicular.

tan($\theta_p$) = $\mu$

Malus' Law:

When completely plane-polarized light of intensity I₀ passes through an analyzer whose transmission axis is inclined at an angle $\theta$ to the polarizer axis, the transmitted intensity I is directly proportional to the square of the cosine of the angle between them:

I = $I_0$ $cos^{2}$($\theta$)

Worked Numerical Example for Revision

Problem: Unpolarized light of intensity I₀ passes through a polarizer. The emerging beam then passes through a second polarizer (analyzer) rotated at 60° relative to the first. Find the final intensity.

Solution:

  1. After passing through the first polarizer, unpolarized light intensity reduces by half: I₁ = I₀ / 2.
  2. Apply Malus' Law for the second polarizer with $\theta$ = 60°: I₂ = I₁ $\cdot$ cos²(60°)
  3. Since \cos(60°) = 1/2, we have cos²(60°) = 1/4.
  4. Final Intensity: I₂ = $\frac{I₀}{2}$ $\cdot$ $\frac{1}{4}$ = $\frac{I₀}{8}$.

JEE/NEET Key Takeaways

  • In YDSE, shifting the apparatus into a liquid of refractive index $\mu$ reduces the fringe width to $\beta$ = $\frac{\beta}{\mu}$.
  • Diffraction requires the obstacle/aperture size (a) to be comparable to the wavelength of light ($\lambda$).
  • Remember that intensity in YDSE goes from 0 to 4I₀, ensuring energy conservation across interference bands.

fields.title: Geometrical Optics: Refraction at Curved Surfaces & Optical Instruments
fields.summary: Refraction at spherical interfaces, compound microscopes, astronomical telescopes, and chromatic aberration formulas
fields.content:
Geometrical optics forms a significant portion of the JEE Main, JEE Advanced, and NEET physics syllabi. Understanding how light rays bend across curved spherical boundaries, as well as how image formation occurs in complex optical instruments like microscopes and telescopes, requires a solid grasp of mathematical derivations, sign conventions, and physical principles. This study guide breaks down spherical refraction, lens behavior, compound microscopes, astronomical telescopes, and chromatic aberrations into actionable concepts for rapid exam revision.

1. Refraction at Spherical Surfaces

When light travels from a medium of refractive index $\mu_1$ to a medium of refractive index $\mu_2$ across a curved spherical interface of radius of curvature R, the relationship between the object distance (u), image distance (v), and R is governed by the single spherical surface refraction formula.

Fundamental Spherical Refraction Formula:

$\frac{\mu_2}{v}$ - $\frac{\mu_1}{u}$ = $\frac{\mu_2 - \mu_1}{R}$

Key Sign Conventions & Assumptions:

  • Light Direction: Light is assumed to travel from left to right. All distances measured in the direction of incident light are positive (+); distances measured opposite to incident light are negative (-).
  • Pole Reference: All distances (u, v, R) are measured from the pole (P) of the spherical surface.
  • Paraxial Rays: The formula strictly holds for paraxial rays—rays making small angles with the principal axis—ensuring that sin($\theta$) & $\approx$ $\theta$ and tan($\theta$) $\approx$ $\theta$.
  • Radius Sign: R is positive (+) for a convex surface presenting towards the rare medium, and negative (-) for a concave surface.

Worked Numerical Example:

Problem: A point object in air ($\mu_1$ = 1.0) is placed 20 cm in front of a concave glass surface ($\mu_2$ = 1.5) of radius of curvature 10 cm. Find the location and nature of the final image.

Solution:

  1. Given: $\mu_1$ = 1.0, $\mu_2$ = 1.5, u = -20 cm, R = -10 cm (since it is concave to incident light).
  2. Apply the formula: $\frac{1.5}{v}$ - $\frac{1.0}{-20}$ = $\frac{\frac{1.5}{1.0}}{-10}$
  3. Simplify: $\frac{1.5}{v}$ + 0.05 = $\frac{0.5}{-10}$ = -0.05
  4. Rearrange: $\frac{1.5}{v}$ = -0.05 - 0.05 = -0.10
  5. Solve for v: v = $\frac{1.5}{-0.10}$ = -15 cm

Conclusion: The image is formed at a distance of 15 cm in front of the surface (on the same side as the object) and is virtual in nature.

2. Compound Microscope

A compound microscope is an optical device used to observe tiny object structures with high angular magnification. It consists of two co-axial convex lenses: the objective lens (short focal length $f_o$, small aperture) and the eyepiece / ocular lens (moderate focal length $f_e$, larger aperture).

Magnifying Power (M) Equations:

The total magnification produced by a compound microscope is the product of the linear magnification of the objective ($m_o$) and the angular magnification of the eyepiece ($m_e$): M = $m_o$ $\times$ $m_e$.

1. Final Image at Least Distance of Distinct Vision (D = 25 cm - Near Point Adjustment):

M = -$\frac{v_o}{u_o}$ $\left(1 + \frac{D}{f_e}\right)$ $\approx$ -$\frac{L}{f_o}$ $\left(1 + \frac{D}{f_e}\right)$

2. Final Image at Infinity (Normal Adjustment / Relaxed Eye):

M = -$\frac{v_o}{u_o}$ $\left(\frac{D}{f_e}\right)$ $\approx$ -$\frac{L}{f_o}$ $\left(\frac{D}{f_e}\right)$

Note on Tube Length (L): The optical tube length L represents the distance between the second focal point of the objective and the first focal point of the eyepiece. The physical separation between the two lenses is given by $v_o$ + |$u_e$|.

3. Astronomical Telescope

An astronomical telescope is used to view distant celestial objects. Unlike a microscope, its objective lens has a large focal length ($f_o$) and a wide aperture to collect maximum light rays, while its eyepiece has a short focal length ($f_e$).

Magnifying Power & Tube Length Formulas:

1. Normal Adjustment (Final Image at Infinity - Minimum Strain):

  • Magnification: M = -$\frac{f_o}{f_e}$
  • Tube Length: L = $f_o$ + $f_e$

2. Near Point Adjustment (Final Image at D):

  • Magnification: M = -$\frac{f_o}{f_e}$ $\left(1 + \frac{f_e}{D}\right)$
  • Tube Length: L = $f_o$ + |$u_e$| = $f_o$ + $\frac{f_e \cdot D}{f_e + D}$

4. Chromatic & Spherical Aberrations

Real single lenses suffer from optical defects known as aberrations, which distort the final image quality:

  • Chromatic Aberrations: Arise because a lens's refractive index varies with the wavelength ($\lambda$) of light (Cauchy's equation). Violet light bends more than red light, causing different colors to focus at different focal points along the principal axis.
    Longitudinal Chromatic Aberration (LCA) = $f_r$ - $f_v$ = $\omega$ $\cdot$ $f_{avg}$ (where $\omega$ is the dispersive power of the lens material).
  • Achromatic Doublets: To eliminate chromatic aberration, a convex lens made of crown glass is combined with a concave lens made of flint glass. The condition for achromatism in contact is:
    $\frac{\omega_1}{f_1}$ + $\frac{\omega_2}{f_2}$ = 0
  • Spherical Aberrations: Marginal rays focus closer to the lens than paraxial rays due to lens curvature. This can be minimized using parabolic mirrors, stops, or combining lenses in contact.

Summary Checklist for JEE/NEET Revision

  • Always double-check Cartesian sign conventions before substituting values into spherical interface equations.
  • For telescopes, high magnification requires $f_o$ $\gt$ $\gt$ $f_e$, whereas for microscopes, high magnification requires small values for both $f_o$ and $f_e$.
  • Remember that normal adjustment yields maximum visual comfort (relaxed eye) at the expense of slightly lower magnification compared to near point adjustment.

fields.title: Potential Energy
fields.variables: PE = Potential energy,  m = Mass,  g = Acceleration due to gravity,  h = Height above surface
fields.description: Energy stored in a body due to its position above ground
fields.when_to_use: When calculating stored energy in raised objects, such as water or reservoirs
fields.mnemonic: “Height times weight” — how much energy is stored just by lifting something up.
fields.example: m = 5 kg, g = 9.8 m/s², h = 3 m. Find PE?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting this assumes CONSTANT g — only a good approximation near a planet's surface, not
for large height changes (use U=−$\frac{GMm}{r}$ instead).
• Forgetting h must be measured from a clearly chosen reference level — PE has no absolute
meaning, only differences matter physically.
• Confusing this with elastic PE ($\frac{1}{2}$kx²) — a completely different storage mechanism.
fields.conceptual_overview: Potential Energy ($U$) represents the scalar stored energy an object possesses due to its position within a uniform gravitational field. It reflects the mechanical work performed against gravitational attraction to elevate a mass to a specific height relative to an arbitrary reference plane
fields.real_world_applications:
Hydroelectric Power Station Design: Calculating potential energy stored in elevated reservoir water volumes to determine electrical power output through turbine generators.

Roller Coaster Physics: Modeling total mechanical energy conservation during gravitational drops to ensure minimum velocity requirements at the top of vertical loops
fields.jee_neet_exam_tips:
Reference Dependence: $U$ depends on the chosen zero-potential reference plane, but potential energy differences ($\Delta U$) are strictly invariant.
Small Altitude Limitation: Valid only when elevation $h \ll R_{\text{Earth}}$ so that local gravity $g$ remains constant.
fields.step_by_step_derivation:
Step 1: Consider a body of mass $m$ lifted vertically upward at constant velocity through height $h$ against gravitational force $F_g = mg$.
Step 2: Express external work done ($W$) by applying force equal and opposite to gravity:$$W = \int_{0}^{h} F_{\text{ext}} \, dh = \int_{0}^{h} mg \, dh$$
Step 3: Evaluate integral assuming uniform acceleration due to gravity $g$:$$W = mg [h]_{0}^{h} = mgh$$
Step 4: Equate external work done to change in gravitational potential energy ($\Delta U$):$$U = mgh$$

fields.title: Ohm's Law
fields.variables: V = Voltage,  I = Electric current,  R = Resistance
fields.description: Voltage(v) across conductor is directly proportional to the curent flowing through it
fields.when_to_use: When designing and analyzing basic resistive circuits and sizing resistors
fields.mnemonic:
“Voltage is the push, resistance is the pushback, current is what gets through” — three ways to
rearrange one relationship
fields.example: I = 2 A, R = 10 Ω. Find V?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting Ohm's law only applies to “ohmic” components with constant R — diodes and hot
filament bulbs are non-ohmic.
• Confusing V (potential difference across a component) with EMF (total voltage supplied, which
may differ due to internal resistance).
• Mixing up which quantity to isolate when rearranging (R=$\frac{V}{I}$ vs I=$\frac{V}{R}$).
fields.conceptual_overview:
Ohm's Law states that the current flowing through an ideal conductor between two points is directly proportional to the potential difference across the two points, provided physical conditions like temperature remain constant.

The constant of proportionality is electrical resistance (R), which quantifies the opposition offered by the material's atomic lattice structure to the flow of free electrons.

While fundamental to linear (ohmic) circuit elements like carbon resistors, non-ohmic components like diodes, transistors, and vacuum tubes deviate from this linear relationship.
fields.real_world_applications:
• Circuit Power Design: Critical for calculating voltage drops, current distribution, and component sizing in PCB and consumer electronics design.
• Electrical Safety Devices: Used to determine trip settings for fuses and circuit breakers during overcurrent situations.
• Sensor Electronics: Forms the working basis for thermistors, strain gauges, and light-dependent resistors (LDRs) that translate physical parameters into measurable voltage signals.
fields.jee_neet_exam_tips:
• Temperature Dependence: Resistance increases with temperature in metallic conductors due to heightened lattice vibrations, causing deviations from linearity.
• Non-Ohmic Devices: Remember semiconductor devices (diodes/LEDs) have non-linear I-V curves and do NOT follow Ohm's Law directly.
• Slope Interpretation: On a V vs I graph, slope represents Resistance (R). On an I vs V graph, slope represents Conductance (1/R).
fields.step_by_step_derivation:
Step 1: Relate drift velocity ($v_d$) of electrons to applied electric field E:
$v_d$ = $\frac{e * E * \tau}{m}$
where e is electron charge, $\tau$ is relaxation time, and m is electron mass.

Step 2: Express electric field E in terms of potential difference V and conductor length L:
E = $\frac{V}{L}$ =>  $v_d$ = $\frac{e * V * \tau}{m * L}$

Step 3: Substitute drift velocity into the fundamental electric current equation I = n * A * e * $v_d$:
I = n * A * e * ($\frac{e * V * \tau}{m * L}$) = $\frac{n * A * e^{2} * \tau}{m * L * V}$

Step 4: Rearrange into V = I * R format, defining Resistance R = $\frac{m * L}{n * A * e^{2} * \tau}$:
V = I * R

fields.title: Momentum
fields.variables: p = Linear momentum,  m = Mass,  v = Velocity
fields.description: It is the quantity of motion possessed by a body.A heavier or faster object has greater momentum
fields.when_to_use: When analyzing collisions, explosions, or any process where momentum conservation applies
fields.mnemonic: “Mass in motion” — momentum combines how much mass is moving and how fast.
fields.example: m = 5 kg, v = 4 m/s. Find p?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting momentum is a VECTOR, in the same direction as velocity.
• Confusing momentum with kinetic energy — both involve mass and velocity, but momentum is
linear in v while KE is quadratic.
• Forgetting momentum, not velocity or KE individually, is what's actually conserved in every
collision.
fields.conceptual_overview:
Linear momentum ($\vec{p}$) is a fundamental vector quantity in classical mechanics that quantifies the quantity of translational motion possessed by a body.

Defined as the product of an object's inertial mass ($m$) and its instantaneous velocity vector ($\vec{v}$), momentum captures both how heavy an object is and how fast it is moving.

In the absence of external net forces ($\sum \vec{F}_{\text{ext}} = 0$), total linear momentum of an isolated system is strictly conserved across all elastic and inelastic collisions.
fields.real_world_applications:
• Rocket Propulsion: Spacecraft accelerate forward by exhausting mass (combustion gas) backward at high speed, conserving total system momentum.
• Vehicle Collision Safety: Crash reconstruction investigators analyze vehicle momentum conservation vectors to compute pre-impact speeds.
• Ballistics & Recoil: Explains firearm kickback action, where forward bullet momentum equals equal and opposite gun recoil momentum.
fields.jee_neet_exam_tips:
• Kinetic Energy Connection: Relate linear momentum p and kinetic energy K using K = $\frac{p^{2}}{2*m}$ or p = $\sqrt{2 * m * K}$.
• Vector Nature: Momentum is a VECTOR. When solving two-dimensional collision problems, resolve momentum independently along X and Y axes $p_x$ = m * $v_x$, $p_y$ = m * $v_y$
• Center of Mass Velocity: Total system momentum equals total mass multiplied by velocity of center of mass: $P_{total}$ = $M_{total}$ * $v_{cm}$.
fields.step_by_step_derivation:
Step 1: Start with Newton's Second Law of Motion asserting force equals mass times acceleration:
F = m * a

Step 2: Substitute acceleration definition a =$\frac{ dv}{dt}$ into equation:
F = m * $\frac{dv}{dt}$

Step 3: Move constant mass m inside time derivative operator:
F = d$\frac{m * v}{dt}$

Step 4: Define quantity inside derivative as linear momentum p:
p = m * v  =>  F = $\frac{dp}{dt}$

fields.title: Newton's First Law of Motion
fields.variables: ΣF = Net external force acting on the body,  a = Resulting acceleration
fields.description: If the net external force acting on a body at rest is zero, the body will remain at rest.
fields.when_to_use: When establishing the concept of inertia and identifying when a body is in equilibrium
fields.mnemonic:
“No net push, no change in motion” — objects don't need a force to keep moving, only to change
how they move.
fields.example:
A hockey puck on frictionless ice experiences zero net horizontal force, so it continues at constant
velocity indefinitely (a conceptual example — no calculation needed).
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting this is about NET force — individual forces (gravity, normal force) can act as long as
they cancel.
• The common misconception that motion itself requires a continuously applied force — it's a
CHANGE in motion that requires one.
• Forgetting “constant velocity” includes the special case of remaining at rest.
fields.conceptual_overview:
Newton's First Law of Motion, also known as the Law of Inertia, states that every body continues in its state of rest or uniform motion in a straight line unless compelled to change that state by an external net force.

Inertia represents the natural resistance of any physical object to changes in its state of velocity. Mass serves as the direct quantitative measure of a body's inertia.

This law establishes the concept of Inertial Reference Frames—coordinate systems moving with constant velocity in which non-accelerated observers measure zero net force on undisturbed bodies.
fields.real_world_applications:
• Automotive Seatbelts & Airbags: Prevents passengers from continuing forward at high velocity due to inertia during sudden vehicle braking.
• Spacecraft Interstellar Cruise: Allows space probes like Voyager to continue traveling through deep space indefinitely at constant speed without burning engine fuel.
• Centrifugal Governors & Flywheels: Uses rotational inertia to stabilize engine speeds against transient load changes.
fields.jee_neet_exam_tips:
• Translational Equilibrium Condition: If net external force Sigma F = 0, acceleration a = 0. This means velocity vector v is CONSTANT (magnitude and direction both unchanging).
• Pseudo Force in Non-Inertial Frames: In frames accelerating with acceleration $a_{frame}$, Newton's laws apply only after applying an imaginary pseudo force $F_{pseudo}$ = -m * $a_{frame}$ opposite to frame acceleration.
• Rest vs Motion Relativity: State of rest (v = 0) and state of uniform motion (v = constant) are physically identical in inertial frames.
fields.step_by_step_derivation:
Step 1: Express Newton's Second Law of Motion relating net force to momentum time rate of change:
$F_{net}$ = $\frac{dp}{dt}$ = $\frac{d(m * v)}{dt}$

Step 2: Assuming constant mass m, express force in terms of acceleration:
$F_{net}$ = m * $\frac{dv}{dt}$ = m * a

Step 3: Set net external force $F_{net}$ equal to zero:
m * a = 0

Step 4: Since mass m is greater than 0, acceleration vector must equal zero:
a = $\frac{dv}{dt}$ = 0  =>  v = constant (State of Rest or Uniform Motion)

fields.title: Gravitational Force
fields.variables: F = Gravitational force,  G = Universal gravitational constant,  m1 , m2  = Interacting masses,  r = Separation distance
fields.description: Force of attraction between two masses.
fields.when_to_use: When calculating attractive forces between celestial bodies, satellites, or everyday masses
fields.mnemonic:
“Newton's original inverse-square law” — every pair of masses attracts, weakening with the
square of distance
fields.common_mistakes:
• Confusing G (a universal constant, always fixed) with g (acceleration due to gravity, which varies
by location).
• Forgetting r is measured between the CENTRES of the two masses, not their surfaces.
• Forgetting this force is always attractive — there's no repulsive gravity in classical mechanics.
fields.conceptual_overview:
Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation states that every point mass attracts every other point mass in the universe by a force acting along the line intersecting both points. This fundamental attractive force is directly proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance separating their centers.

As a fundamental conservative force in classical mechanics, gravity governs celestial dynamics, orbital motion, planetary trajectories, and tidal forces. Unlike electrostatic or magnetic forces, gravitational force is strictly attractive and operates across infinite distances, though its intensity diminishes rapidly following the inverse-square law.

The universal gravitational constant (G = 6.674 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg²) serves as the constant of proportionality across all physical scales, from subatomic interactions to cosmic galaxy clusters.
fields.real_world_applications:
• Satellite Orbit & Trajectory Calculations: Essential for determining geostationary, low-Earth orbit (LEO), and escape trajectories for artificial satellites and space probes.
• Celestial Mechanics & Astronomy: Used by astrophysicists to model planetary orbits, binary star systems, lunar tides, and galactic structure.
• Gravitational Lensing & Dark Matter Estimation: Helps astronomical research measure massive celestial objects by studying the gravitational deflection of light.
• Ocean Tides Prediction: Explains the gravitational interaction between the Earth, Moon, and Sun responsible for high and low ocean tides worldwide.
fields.jee_neet_exam_tips:
• Center-to-Center Distance Traps: Always measure the separation distance r from the CENTRES of mass of the two spherical bodies, not from their surfaces.
• Distinguish G vs g: Universal Gravitational Constant G (6.674 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg²) remains fixed everywhere in the universe, whereas local acceleration due to gravity g (9.8 m/s²) changes with altitude, depth, and planet mass.
• Inverse-Square Proportionality: Doubling the distance r decreases the gravitational force F by a factor of 4 (1/2²). Tripling distance reduces force to 1/9th.
• Vector Form & Sign Conventions: Gravitational force is a vector quantity pointing inward toward the attracting mass center. Use vector notation F = -$\frac{G*M1*M2}{r^{2}}$ * $\hat{r}$ for coordinate-based numericals.
• Superposition Principle: When dealing with multiple point masses, calculate individual gravitational force vectors independently and sum them vectorially using component resolution.
fields.step_by_step_derivation:
Step 1: Express fundamental proportionalities established by Sir Isaac Newton:
Force is proportional to the product of masses: F ∝ (m1 * m2)
Force is inversely proportional to the square of distance: F ∝ $\frac{1}{r^{2}}$

Step 2: Combine the proportional relationships into a single proportional expression:
F ∝ $\frac{m1 * m2}{r^{2}}$

Step 3: Introduce the Universal Gravitational Constant (G) as the constant of proportionality to convert the relationship into an exact equation:
F = $\frac{G * m1 * m2}{r^{2}}$

Step 4: Dimensional Analysis Verification:
[F] = [G] * [M]² * [L]⁻²
[M L T⁻²] = [M⁻¹ L³ T⁻²] * [M²] * [L⁻²] = [M L T⁻²]
The dimensions match on both sides, proving the mathematical consistency of the gravitational force formula.

fields.title: Escape Velocity
fields.variables: v = Escape velocity,  G = Universal gravitational constant,  M = Mass of celestial body, R = Radius of celestial body
fields.description: Minimum Velocity(v) to escape Earth's gravity(gR)
fields.when_to_use: When calculating the launch speed needed for spacecraft to leave a planet's or moon's gravitational field
fields.mnemonic: “√2 times faster than orbital velocity” — escaping needs more speed than merely orbiting.
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting escape velocity is independent of the mass of the escaping object itself.
• Forgetting this is the MINIMUM speed needed with no further propulsion — real spacecraft often
use more complex trajectories.
• Confusing this with orbital velocity, which is smaller by a factor of √2.
fields.conceptual_overview:
Escape velocity represents the minimum initial speed required for a free, non-propelled body to escape permanently from the gravitational influence of a primary massive astronomical body without further propulsion.

At this threshold speed, the kinetic energy of the projectile equals its magnitude of negative gravitational potential energy. This results in zero total mechanical energy, placing the object on a parabolic trajectory that brings it to rest only at an infinite distance from the parent mass.

Crucially, escape velocity depends exclusively on the mass (M) and radius (R) of the primary body, remaining completely independent of the mass or direction of projection of the escaping object.
fields.real_world_applications:
• Spaceflight Launch Architecture: Used to calculate energy requirements and multi-stage fuel loads for planetary probes like Mars rovers and interstellar missions.
• Stellar Collapse & Black Hole Horizons: Defines the event horizon radius (Schwarzschild radius) where the required escape velocity reaches or exceeds the speed of light.
• Planetary Atmospheric Retention: Explains why small bodies like the Moon lack atmospheres (low escape velocity allows gas molecules to bleed into space), while gas giants retain light elements like Hydrogen and Helium.
fields.jee_neet_exam_tips:
• Earth-Specific Value: Remember Earth's surface escape velocity is approximately 11.2 km/s (or 11,200 m/s).
• Mass Independence: A 1 kg satellite and a 10,000 kg rocket require the EXACT same escape velocity from the same location.
• Angle Independence: The angle of projection theta does not affect escape speed (unless atmospheric drag is considered, which is ignored in ideal questions).
• Surface Acceleration Formula Alternative: You can rewrite escape velocity using surface gravity g as v = $\sqrt{2 * g * R}$.
fields.step_by_step_derivation:
Step 1: Apply Conservation of Mechanical Energy between surface projection point (1) and infinite distance (2):
$E_{initial}$ = $E_{final}$

Step 2: Write total kinetic and potential energy equations:
$K_1$ + $U_1$ =$K_2$ + $U_2$
$\frac{1}{2}$ * m * $v^{2}$ - $\frac{G * M * m}{R}$ = 0 + 0

Step 3: Equate surface kinetic energy to gravitational potential energy magnitude:
$\frac{1}{2}$ * m * $v^{2}$ = $\frac{G * M * m}{R}$

Step 4: Cancel object mass (m) on both sides and solve for velocity v:
$v^{2}$ = $\frac{2 * G * M}{R}$
v = $\sqrt{\frac{2 * G * M}{R}}$

fields.title: Electric Charge
fields.variables: Q = Electric charge,  I = Electric current,  t = Time
fields.description: Charge flowing through a Conductor.
fields.when_to_use: When calculating total charge delivered in charging batteries or through a circuit over time
fields.mnemonic:
“Steady current over time adds up to charge” — charge is current multiplied (or integrated) over
time.
fields.example: I = 3 A, t = 10 s. Find Q?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting this simple multiplication only works for CONSTANT current — varying current needs
the area under an I-t graph.
• Confusing Q (total charge, coulombs) with I (rate of flow, amperes).
• Forgetting conventional current direction is opposite to actual electron flow in a wire.
fields.conceptual_overview:
Electric charge ($Q$) is the fundamental intrinsic physical property of matter that causes it to experience a force when placed in an electromagnetic field.

Quantized fundamentally in discrete integer multiples of the elementary electronic charge ($e \approx 1.602 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$), charge exists in two complementary polarities: positive and negative.

By fundamental definition of steady electric current ($I$) as net charge flow per unit time, total charge transferred across a conductor cross-section over time interval $t$ equals the product of current and time.
fields.real_world_applications:
• Battery Capacity Ratings: Stored electrochemical charge capacity in commercial batteries is rated directly in Ampere-hours (Ah) or milliampere-hours (mAh).
• Electrostatic Spray Painting: Charges paint droplets positively so they spread uniformly and adhere strongly to grounded metal surfaces.
• Electrostatic Precipitators: Uses high-voltage charging electrodes to collect airborne ash and pollutant particles from industrial smokestacks.
fields.jee_neet_exam_tips:
• Quantization Principle: Charge on any body is always an integral multiple of elementary charge: Q = ±n*e (where n = 1, 2, 3...). Fractional charges (like quarks) do not exist in free form.
• Conservation of Charge: Total electric charge in an isolated system remains strictly constant during all chemical, physical, and nuclear processes.
• Time-Varying Current Integration: If electric current varies with time, total charge is calculated by integrating current over time: Q = $\int I dt$.
fields.step_by_step_derivation:
Step 1: Define average electric current $I_{avg}$ as net charge $\Delta$ Q passing through a cross-sectional area per time $\Delta$ t:
$I_{avg}$ = $\frac{\Delta Q}{\Delta t}$

Step 2: Take limit as time interval approaches zero for instantaneous current I:
I = $\frac{dq}{dt}$

Step 3: Separate variables to express differential charge dq:
dq = I * dt

Step 4: Integrate over time interval from t = 0 to t = T under steady, constant current I:
Q = $\int_{0}^{T}$ I dt = I * $\int_{0}^{T}$ dt = I * t

fields.title: Electric Power
fields.variables: P = Electric power,  V = Voltage,  I = Current
fields.description: Rate of electrical energy consumption.
fields.when_to_use: When rating electrical appliances, calculating energy bills, or sizing circuit components
fields.mnemonic:
“Voltage times current, the electrical workhorse formula” — the electrical analogue of P=Fv in
mechanics.
fields.example: V = 220 V, I = 5 A. Find P?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting this is the same underlying relationship as P=I²R=$\frac{V²}{R}$ for purely resistive loads.
• Forgetting AC circuits with a phase difference between V and I need an extra power-factor term:
P=VIcosφ.
• Confusing instantaneous/average power with total energy consumed, which requires multiplying
by time.
fields.conceptual_overview:
Electric power is the rate per unit time at which electrical energy is transferred, delivered, or converted by an electric circuit element.

When an electric potential difference (V) drives a steady current (I) of charges through a circuit component, work is performed on those charges. The total power consumed or delivered equals the product of potential difference across the terminal and current passing through it.

Depending on whether a device absorbs or supplies power, electric components are classified as passive loads (consuming power) or active sources (supplying power) in dynamic network analysis.
fields.real_world_applications:
• Utility Energy Metering: Forms the underlying metric for billing electricity consumption measured in Kilowatt-hours (kWh = 1000 Watts maintained for 1 hour).
