Step 4: Substitute current definition I = n * A * e * $v_d$ into the total force equation:
F = (n * A * e * $v_d$) * B * L * sin($\theta$) = I * B * L * sin($\theta$) = B * I * L * sin($\theta$)

fields.title: Magnetic Field of Solenoid
fields.variables: B = Magnetic field,   μ₀ = Permeability of free space,  I = Electric current, n = Number of turns
fields.description: Uniform magnetic field inside a long solenoid
fields.when_to_use: When designing electromagnets, inductors or magnetic field source for laboratory experiments
fields.given_by: direct consequence of Ampère's Law — remarkably, the magnetic field inside an ideal solenoid is uniform throughout its interior and zero outside, regardless of the coil's diameter
fields.mnemonic: “Turns per length, times current” — n here means turns PER UNIT LENGTH, not total turns.
fields.example: n = 1000 turns/m, I = 2 A. Find B?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Using total turns N instead of turns-per-length n — a very common mix-up.
• Forgetting this formula gives B only deep inside a long (ideal) solenoid, well away from the ends.
• Forgetting the field just outside an ideal solenoid is essentially zero.
fields.conceptual_overview: The magnetic field inside an infinitely long, tightly wound helical solenoid is exceptionally uniform, parallel to the central longitudinal axis, and nearly zero outside the coil windings. The field intensity depends directly on the core permeability ($\mu_0$), linear turn density ($n$), and current ($I$)
fields.real_world_applications:
Electromechanical Actuators: Driving industrial solenoid valves for automated hydraulic control.

MRI Superconducting Magnets: Generating strong uniform magnetic fields for high-resolution diagnostic diagnostic imaging
fields.jee_neet_exam_tips:
Finite Solenoid Formula:$$B = \frac{\mu_0 n I}{2} (\cos\theta_1 - \cos\theta_2)$$
End-Point Edge Value: At the extreme edge along the central axis of a long solenoid, field strength drops to exactly half:$$B_{\text{end}} = \frac{1}{2} \mu_0 n I$$
fields.step_by_step_derivation:
Step 1: Construct a rectangular Amperian loop $abcd$ of length $L$ with side $ab$ inside the core and side $cd$ outside.
Step 2: Apply Ampère’s Circuital Law ($\oint \vec{B} \cdot d\vec{l} = \mu_0 I_{\text{enclosed}}$):$$\int_{a}^{b} \vec{B} \cdot d\vec{l} + \int_{b}^{c} \vec{B} \cdot d\vec{l} + \int_{c}^{d} \vec{B} \cdot d\vec{l} + \int_{d}^{a} \vec{B} \cdot d\vec{l} = \mu_0 (N I)$$
Step 3: Evaluate integrals ($B = 0$ outside; $\vec{B} \perp d\vec{l}$ on sides $bc, da$):$$B \cdot L + 0 + 0 + 0 = \mu_0 (N I)$$
Step 4: Define turn density $n = \frac{N}{L}$:$$B = \mu_0 \left(\frac{N}{L}\right) I = \mu_0 n I$$

fields.title: Energy stored in Inductor
fields.variables: U = Stored magnetic energy,  L = Self-inductance,  I = Current through  inductor
fields.description: Energy stored in the magnetic field of an inductor
fields.when_to_use: When designing energy storage in chokes, transformers
fields.given_by: by integrating the power delivered to an inductor (P = Li di/dt) as current rises from zero to I — the magnetic counterpart to energy stored in a capacitor's electric field
fields.mnemonic: “Same shape as kinetic energy, but L replaces m and I replaces v.”
fields.example: L = 2 H, I = 3 A. Find U?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting the $\frac{1}{2}$ factor at the front.
• Confusing this stored magnetic energy with a capacitor's stored energy (U = $\frac{1}{2}$CV²) — similar
shape, different circuit element entirely.
• Forgetting this energy returns to the circuit as current decreases — it isn't dissipated like
resistive heating.
fields.conceptual_overview: An inductor stores energy within its internal magnetic field when an electric current flows through its windings. Opposing current changes via self-induced back electromotive force (EMF), the inductor converts electrical work into stored magnetic potential energy
fields.real_world_applications:
Switch-Mode Power Supplies (SMPS): Storing energy during buck-boost converter switching cycles.

Automotive Ignition Coils: Storing magnetic energy to generate high-voltage discharge sparks across engine spark plugs
fields.jee_neet_exam_tips:
Magnetic Energy Density ($u_B$): Energy stored per unit volume in a magnetic field:$$u_B = \frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}$$
LC Circuit Energy Conservation: Ideal LC circuits continuously oscillate energy between inductive field ($\frac{1}{2}LI^2$) and capacitive field ($\frac{q^2}{2C}$).
fields.step_by_step_derivation:
Step 1: Express self-induced back EMF magnitude during current buildup:$$\mathcal{E} = L \frac{dI}{dt}$$
Step 2: Calculate instantaneous power supplied against back EMF ($P = \mathcal{E} I$):$$P = L I \frac{dI}{dt}$$
Step 3: Express work done $dW$ in incremental time interval $dt$:$$dW = P \, dt = L I \, dI$$
Step 4: Integrate work from zero current to final steady value $I$:$$U = \int_{0}^{I} L I \, dI = \frac{1}{2} L I^2$$

fields.title: Photoelectric Effect
fields.variables: KE_max = Maximum kinetic energy of emitted electrons,  h = Planck's constant,  f = Frequency of incident light,  ϕ = Work function of metal
fields.description: Maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons ejected from a metal surface.
fields.when_to_use: When analyzing photodetectors, solar cells or threshold behaviour of light-induced electrons
fields.given_by: Albert Einstein's 1905 explanation of the photoelectric effect — proposed that light behaves as discrete energy packets (photons), each capable of ejecting an electron only if its energy exceeds the metal's work function. This work, not relativity, earned him the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics
fields.mnemonic:
“Photon pays the toll” — hf is what's delivered, φ is the toll (work function) to escape, whatever's
left is kinetic energy
fields.example: f = 1×$10^{15}$ Hz, φ = 2 eV. Find $KE_{max}$?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting KEmax
 is zero (no photoemission at all) whenever hf < φ, no matter how intense the light is.
• Confusing intensity (affects the NUMBER of photoelectrons) with frequency (affects EACH
photon's energy and thus KEmax
) — a very commonly tested distinction.
• Forgetting the work function φ is a material property that differs for every metal.
fields.conceptual_overview: Einstein’s Photoelectric Equation models light absorption as localized discrete energy quanta (photons). When an incident photon of frequency $\nu$ hits a metal surface, its full energy ($h\nu$) is absorbed by a single bound electron. Part of this energy overcomes the metallic work function ($\phi$), while the remainder converts into the electron's maximum kinetic energy ($K_{\max}$)
fields.real_world_applications:
Photomultiplier Tubes (PMT): Detecting low-level optical signals in high-energy particle physics experiments.

Light Intensity Sensors: Controlling automated streetlight activation and camera exposure meters
fields.jee_neet_exam_tips:
Universal Graph Slope: The slope of stopping potential ($V_s$) versus frequency ($\nu$) is a universal constant equal to $\frac{h}{e}$.
Intensity Independence: Maximum kinetic energy ($K_{\max}$) and stopping potential ($V_s$) depend only on incident frequency ($\nu$), completely independent of light beam intensity.
fields.step_by_step_derivation:
Step 1: State conservation of energy for a single photon-electron collision:$$E_{	ext{photon}} = 	ext{Work Function} + 	ext{Maximum Kinetic Energy}$$
Step 2: Substitute photon energy $E = h
u$ and threshold frequency expression $\phi = h
u_0$:$$h
u = \phi + K_{\max} = h
u_0 +  rac{1}{2} m v_{\max}^2$$
Step 3: Express in terms of stopping potential ($V_s$), where $K_{\max} = e V_s$:$$e V_s = h
u - h
u_0 \implies Vj_s = \left( rac{h}{e}ight)
u -  rac{\phi}{e}$$

fields.title: Mass-Energy Equivalence
fields.variables: E = Energy equivalent,  m = Mass,  c = Speed of light
fields.description: A small amount of Mass(m) can generate Large amount of Energy(E)
fields.when_to_use: When calculating energy released in nuclear fission, fusion
fields.mnemonic:
“Mass IS energy, just wearing a costume” — even a tiny mass corresponds to an enormous
energy because c² is so large.
fields.example: m = 1 g = 0.001 kg. Find E?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting c must be in m/s (3×$10^{8}$), not km/s or any other unit, for E to come out in joules.
• Forgetting this gives the maximum theoretical energy locked in a mass — practical processes
(like nuclear reactions) only release 
a small fraction of it.
• Confusing this general relation with the Q-value formula, which computes released energy from
a specific mass DIFFERENCE (Δm), not total mass.
fields.conceptual_overview: Albert Einstein's Mass-Energy Equivalence principle establishes that mass and energy are interchangeable manifestations of the same physical quantity. A rest mass ($m_0$) contains intrinsic rest energy, and any change in a bound system's mass ($\Delta m$) releases or absorbs an equivalent quantity of energy ($\Delta E$)
fields.real_world_applications:
Nuclear Power Reactors: Converting mass defect into thermal energy during Uranium-235 fission events
Positron Emission Tomography (PET Scans): Converting electron-positron annihilation mass into pairs of $511\text{ keV}$ gamma-ray photons for medical imaging.
fields.jee_neet_exam_tips:
Atomic Mass Unit Equivalent Shortcut:$$1\text{ amu (u)} \equiv 931.5 \text{ MeV}$$
Relativistic Momentum-Energy Relation:$$E^2 = (pc)^2 + (m_0 c^2)^2$$
fields.step_by_step_derivation:
Step 1: Express relativistic momentum for speed $v$:$$p = \gamma m_0 v = \frac{m_0 v}{\sqrt{1 - \frac{v^2}{c^2}}}$$
Step 2: Apply relativistic force differential $F = \frac{dp}{dt}$ to work done formula ($dW = F \, ds = v \, dp$):$$dW = v \, d\left( \frac{m_0 v}{\sqrt{1 - \frac{v^2}{c^2}}} \right) = c^2 \, dm$$
Step 3: Integrate work done from rest mass $m_0$ to dynamic mass $m$:$$E_K = \int_{m_0}^{m} c^2 \, dm = (m - m_0)c^2$$
Step 4: Define total relativistic energy ($E = E_K + m_0 c^2$):$$E = m c^2$$

fields.title: Bohr's Energy (nth Orbit)
fields.variables: E_n = Energy of electron in nth orbit,  Z = Atomic number,  n = Principal quantum number
fields.description: Energy of an electron in nth orbit of hydrogen atom.
fields.when_to_use: When calculating spectral lines energies or ionization energies of hydrogen-like atoms
fields.mnemonic:
“Deeper orbit, deeper energy well” — energy becomes more negative (more tightly bound) as n
decreases.
fields.example:
Hydrogen (Z=1), n=2. Find E2
?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting the Z² factor for hydrogen-like ions with more than one proton (He+, Li2+) — the
formula reduces to −$\frac{13.6}{n²}$ only for plain hydrogen.
• Forgetting energy is always negative for a bound electron, with n=∞ corresponding to E=0 (a
free electron).
• Confusing the orbit index n with the number of electrons or protons in the atom.
fields.conceptual_overview: Niels Bohr's model quantifies the total energy ($E_n$) of an electron revolving in stable non-radiating circular orbits around a hydrogen-like single-electron nucleus. Quantizing electron angular momentum ($L = \frac{nh}{2\pi}$) yields discrete electronic energy levels that explain atomic emission spectra
fields.real_world_applications:
Semiconductor Quantum Dots: Tuning absorption and fluorescence emission spectra by engineering nanoscale confinement dimensions.

Gas Discharge Lasers: Selecting optical pumping levels in Helium-Neon and Argon-ion laser systems
fields.jee_neet_exam_tips:
Energy Ratio Relationships:$$K_n = -E_n, \quad U_n = 2 E_n$$
Hydrogen Ground State ($Z=1, n=1$): $E_1 = -13.6\text{ eV}$.
Ionization Energy Shortcut: Energy required to remove an electron from orbit $n$ to infinity is $+E_n$.
fields.step_by_step_derivation:
Step 1: Equate electrostatic attraction to required centripetal force for radius $r$:$$\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{Z e^2}{r^2} = \frac{m v^2}{r} \implies m v^2 = \frac{Z e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r}$$
Step 2: Express total mechanical energy ($E = K + U$):$$K = \frac{1}{2} m v^2 = \frac{Z e^2}{8\pi\varepsilon_0 r}, \quad U = -\frac{Z e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r} \implies E = -\frac{Z e^2}{8\pi\varepsilon_0 r}$$

Step 3: Substitute Bohr’s quantized radius ($r_n = \frac{n^2 h^2 \varepsilon_0}{\pi m Z e^2}$):$$E_n = -\frac{m Z^2 e^4}{8 \varepsilon_0^2 h^2 n^2}$$
Step 4: Substitute physical constants ($m, e, \varepsilon_0, h$) and convert Joules to electron-volts ($\text{eV}$):$$E_n = -\frac{13.6 Z^2}{n^2} \text{ eV}$$

fields.title: Radioactive Decay Law
fields.variables: N = Number of undecayed nuclei at time t,  N_0 = Initial number of nuclei,  λ = Decay constant,  t = Elapsed time
fields.description: Number of radioactive nuclei remaining  after time t.
fields.when_to_use: When modelling carbon dating, nuclear medicine dosing
fields.given_by: Ernest Rutherford and Frederick Soddy while studying thorium decay — established that radioactive substances decay exponentially over time, with the rate of decay proportional to the amount of substance remaining
fields.mnemonic:
“Exponential fade, never quite zero” — the remaining amount decreases smoothly and never
actually reaches zero in finite time.
fields.example: $N_0$ = 1000 atoms, λ = 0.1/s, t = 10 s. Find N?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting λ and half-life are related by $t_{\frac{1}{2}}$ = $\frac{0.693}{λ}$ — easy to mix up which one a problem
 actually gives.
• Forgetting this describes an average/statistical trend over a large number of atoms — for a
small sample, actual decay is random and doesn't trace this smooth curve exactly.
• Forgetting activity A = λN follows the same exponential decay as N itself.
fields.conceptual_overview: The Radioactive Decay Law describes the exponential decrease over time in the number of undecayed nuclei within an unstable isotope sample. It operates as a purely statistical process where the rate of decay is proportional to the total number of active radioactive nuclei present at that instant
fields.real_world_applications:
Radiocarbon Dating: Determining the age of organic artifacts by measuring Carbon-14 residual activity decay.

Nuclear Waste Shielding Logistics: Modeling activity reduction over centuries for spent fuel storage vaults
fields.jee_neet_exam_tips:
Activity Relation ($A = -\frac{dN}{dt}$):$$A(t) = A_0 e^{-\lambda t} \quad \text{where } A_0 = \lambda N_0$$
Half-Life Fraction Shortcut: After $k$ half-lives ($t = k \cdot T_{1/2}$), the remaining fraction of active nuclei is:$$\frac{N}{N_0} = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^k$$
fields.step_by_step_derivation:
Step 1: State fundamental rate proportionality, where $\lambda$ is the decay constant:$$-\frac{dN}{dt} \propto N \implies -\frac{dN}{dt} = \lambda N$$
Step 2: Separate variables for integration:$$\frac{dN}{N} = -\lambda \, dt$$
Step 3: Integrate from time $t = 0$ (initial count $N_0$) to time $t$ (remaining count $N$):$$\int_{N_0}^{N} \frac{dN}{N} = -\int_{0}^{t} \lambda \, dt \implies \ln\left(\frac{N}{N_0}\right) = -\lambda t$$
Step 4: Take the exponential of both sides:$$N(t) = N_0 e^{-\lambda t}$$

fields.title: Half-Life
fields.variables: t_1/2 = Half-life of a radioactive substance,  λ = Decay constant of a radioactive substance
fields.description: Time required  for half the radioactive nuclei to decay
fields.when_to_use: When estimating the age of radioactive samples or predicting decay timeline of isotopes
fields.given_by: Ernest Rutherford and Frederick Soddy in their early studies of radioactive decay — describes the time required for exactly half of a radioactive sample's nuclei to decay, regardless of the initial quantity
fields.mnemonic:
“0.693 is just ln(2) in disguise” — half-life falls directly out of solving N=N0
/2 in the decay
equation
fields.example: λ = 0.05 per year. Find the half-life?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting 0.693 is just an approximation of ln(2) ≈ 0.6931 — more decimal places give a
 slightly more precise answer.
• Confusing half-life with mean lifetime (τ = $\frac{1}{λ}$), which is a different, larger quantity.
• Forgetting half-life is constant for a given isotope, independent of how much substance is
currently present.
fields.conceptual_overview: The Half-Life Period ($T_{1/2}$) is the time duration required for half of the radioactive parent nuclei in a sample to decay into daughter products. It is a constant intrinsic property of each specific radionuclide, remaining independent of initial sample quantity, ambient temperature, or pressure
fields.real_world_applications:
Nuclear Medicine Dosimetry: Selecting short half-life diagnostic radioisotopes (e.g., Technetium-99m, $T_{1/2} \approx 6 \text{ hours}$) to minimize patient radiation exposure.
Smoke Detector Maintenance: Utilizing Americium-241 ($T_{1/2} = 432 \text{ years}$) for constant ionization levels over long operating lifetimes.
fields.jee_neet_exam_tips:
Mean / Average Life ($\tau$): Average lifespan of a radioactive nucleus:$$\tau = \frac{1}{\lambda} = \frac{T_{1/2}}{\ln 2} \approx 1.44 T_{1/2}$$
Decay Percentage Shortcut:After $1 \cdot T_{1/2}$: $50\%$ remains ($50\%$ decayed).
After $2 \cdot T_{1/2}$: $25\%$ remains ($75\%$ decayed).
After $3 \cdot T_{1/2}$: $12.5\%$ remains ($87.5\%$ decayed).
After $10 \cdot T_{1/2}$: $\approx 0.1\%$ remains ($99.9\%$ decayed).
fields.step_by_step_derivation:
Step 1: Substitute condition $N(T_{1/2}) = \frac{N_0}{2}$ into the Radioactive Decay Law:$$\frac{N_0}{2} = N_0 e^{-\lambda T_{1/2}}$$
Step 2: Divide by $N_0$ and invert both sides:$$\frac{1}{2} = e^{-\lambda T_{1/2}} \implies 2 = e^{\lambda T_{1/2}}$$
Step 3: Take the natural logarithm ($\ln$) of both sides:$$\ln(2) = \lambda T_{1/2}$$
Step 4: Isolate half-life $T_{1/2}$ using $\ln(2) \approx 0.69315$:$$T_{1/2} = \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda} \approx \frac{0.693}{\lambda}$$

fields.title: First Equation of Motion
fields.variables: v = Final velocity,  u = Initial velocity,  a = Uniform acceleration,  t = Time
fields.description: This equation relates the final velocity of an object to its initial velocity, acceleration, and the time for which it has been accelerating.
fields.when_to_use: When solving straight line motion involving constant acceleration
fields.mnemonic:
“The one without displacement” — useful exactly when a problem doesn't mention or ask about
distance.
fields.example: u = 5 m/s, a = 2 m/s², t = 4 s. Find v?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting a is negative for deceleration — sign convention matters relative to the direction of
initial velocity.
• Confusing this with average velocity — this gives the instantaneous final velocity, not an average.
• Assuming u must be zero — it can be any nonzero initial velocity.
fields.conceptual_overview: The First and Third Equations of Motion describe linear kinematics under constant, uniform acceleration ($a$). The first equation determines instantaneous velocity ($v$) as a function of time ($t$), while the third equation provides a time-independent velocity-displacement relationship derived from mechanical work-energy principles
fields.real_world_applications:
Aircraft Runway Length Design: Calculating minimum required landing strip length based on aircraft touchdown speeds and reverse-thrust deceleration rates.

Elevator Acceleration Profiling: Designing smooth, uniform acceleration curves for high-rise elevator traction systems
fields.jee_neet_exam_tips:
Stopping Distance Shortcut: If a car moving at velocity $u$ stops in distance $s$ under constant braking force, doubling initial speed ($2u$) quadruples stopping distance ($4s$) because $s \propto u^2$
Max Height in Vertical Projection ($v = 0, a = -g$):$$H_{\max} = \frac{u^2}{2g}, \quad t_{\text{ascent}} = \frac{u}{g}$$
fields.step_by_step_derivation:
Step 1 (First Equation): Integrate constant acceleration definition $a = \frac{dv}{dt}$:$$\int_{u}^{v} dv = \int_{0}^{t} a \, dt \implies v - u = at \implies v = u + at$$
Step 2 (Third Equation): Express acceleration using the chain rule:$$a = \frac{dv}{dt} = \frac{dv}{ds} \cdot \frac{ds}{dt} = v \frac{dv}{ds}$$
Step 3: Separate variables and integrate from initial state $(u, 0)$ to final state $(v, s)$:$$\int_{u}^{v} v \, dv = \int_{0}^{s} a \, ds$$
Step 4: Evaluate the integrals:$$\left[ \frac{v^2}{2} \right]_{u}^{v} = a [s]_{0}^{s} \implies \frac{v^2 - u^2}{2} = as \implies v^2 = u^2 + 2as$$

fields.title: Range of Projectile (horizontal)
fields.variables: R = Horizontal range,  u = Initial velocity,  θ = Angle of projection,  g = Acceleration due to gravity
fields.description: The maximum horizontal distance(R) covered by a projectile.
fields.when_to_use: When predicting landing distance of projectile motion problems such as ball games or artillery trajectories
fields.mnemonic: “45 degrees wins” — range is maximized at θ=45°, since sin(2×45°) = sin90° = 1.
fields.example: u = 20 m/s, θ = 30°, g = 10 m/s². Find R?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting the angle inside the formula is doubled (2θ), not just θ — a very common slip.
• Forgetting this assumes the projectile lands at the same height it launched from — different
launch/landing heights need the full trajectory equations.
• Ignoring that air resistance is neglected here — real projectiles land shorter than this formula
predicts.
fields.conceptual_overview: The horizontal range ($R$) of a projectile measures the total horizontal distance traveled from its launch point to where it returns to its original vertical level. Under uniform gravity and negligible air resistance, horizontal velocity remains constant throughout the trajectory while gravity acts strictly along the vertical direction
fields.real_world_applications:
Ballistic Artillery Targeting: Computing gun elevation angles needed to hit distant targets in military ballistics.

Athletic Performance Optimization: Calculating optimal launch angles for maximum horizontal throw in javelin, shot put, and long jump
fields.jee_neet_exam_tips:
Maximum Range Condition: $R_{\max} = \frac{u^2}{g}$ occurs at projection angle $\theta = 45^\circ$
Complementary Angle Identity: Projection angles $\theta$ and $(90^\circ - \theta)$ yield identical horizontal ranges for the same initial speed $u$
Range-Height Relation Shortcut:$$\frac{R}{H_{\max}} = 4 \cot\theta$$
fields.step_by_step_derivation:
Step 1: Resolve initial velocity $u$ at angle $\theta$ into horizontal and vertical components:$$u_x = u \cos\theta, \quad u_y = u \sin\theta$$
Step 2: Calculate total time of flight ($T$) by setting vertical displacement $y = 0$:$$y = u_y T - \frac{1}{2} g T^2 = 0 \implies T = \frac{2u \sin\theta}{g}$$
Step 3: Calculate horizontal range $R$ by multiplying uniform horizontal speed by time of flight:$$R = u_x \cdot T = (u \cos\theta) \cdot \left(\frac{2u \sin\theta}{g}\right) = \frac{u^2 (2 \sin\theta \cos\theta)}{g}$$
Step 4: Substitute trigonometric double-angle identity ($2\sin\theta\cos\theta = \sin 2\theta$):$$R = \frac{u^2 \sin 2\theta}{g}$$

fields.title: Centripetal Acceleration
fields.variables: a = Centripetal acceleration,  v = Velocity of a body,  r = Radius of circular path
fields.description: The acceleration(a) of an object moving in a circular path, directed towards the center of the circle.
fields.when_to_use: When analyzing object moving in circles, such as vehicle rounding bends or satellites in orbit
fields.mnemonic:
“Tighter turn or faster speed, harder pull toward the centre” — a grows with v squared but only
inversely with r
fields.worked_example: v = 10 m/s, r = 5 m. Find a?
fields.example: v = 10 m/s, r = 5 m. Find a?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting this acceleration always points toward the centre of the circular path, never along
 the direction of motion.
• Forgetting a real net force (centripetal force = $\frac{mv²}{r}$) must supply this acceleration — it doesn't
appear on its own.
• Confusing this with tangential acceleration, which changes speed rather than direction and is
an entirely separate quantity.
fields.conceptual_overview: Centripetal acceleration ($a_c$) defines the continuous rate of change of velocity direction for an object following a curved or circular path of radius $r$. Always directed radially inward toward the center of curvature, it is required for circular motion even when tangential speed ($v$) remains constant
fields.real_world_applications:
Medical Laboratory Centrifuges: Separating blood plasma components using ultra-high rotational acceleration fields.

Highway Curve Design: Calculating minimum radii for highway exit ramps to prevent high-speed vehicle skidding
fields.jee_neet_exam_tips:
Work Done by Centripetal Force: Always zero ($W = 0$) because centripetal force is strictly perpendicular to velocity displacement ($\vec{F}_c \perp d\vec{r}$)
Non-Uniform Circular Motion Net Acceleration:$$a_{\text{net}} = \sqrt{a_c^2 + a_t^2} \quad \text{where } a_t = \frac{dv}{dt} = r\alpha$$
fields.step_by_step_derivation:
Step 1: Express circular motion position vector in polar coordinates: $\vec{r} = r \hat{r}$
Step 2: Differentiate position vector with respect to time to get velocity:$$\vec{v} = \frac{d\vec{r}}{dt} = r \omega \hat{\theta}$$
Step 3: Differentiate velocity vector with respect to time to get acceleration:$$\vec{a} = \frac{d\vec{v}}{dt} = \frac{d}{dt}(r \omega \hat{\theta}) = r \alpha \hat{\theta} + r \omega \left(\frac{d\hat{\theta}}{dt}\right)$$
Step 4: Substitute unit vector derivative $\frac{d\hat{\theta}}{dt} = -\omega \hat{r}$. For constant angular speed ($\alpha = 0$), radial acceleration vector is:$$\vec{a}_c = -\omega^2 r \hat{r} \implies a_c = \omega^2 r = \frac{v^2}{r}$$

fields.title: Work-Energy Theorem
fields.variables: W,ΔKE = Net work done,  m = Mass,  v1,v2 = Initial and final speeds
fields.description: The work done(W) on an object is equal to the change in its kinetic energy.(ΔK.E)
fields.when_to_use: When relating forces acting over a distance to resulting change in an object's speed
fields.given_by: tracing how a force, acting through a displacement, doesn't vanish into nothing but transforms entirely into the energy of motion — bridging the language of forces with the language of speed
fields.mnemonic:
“Net work is exactly the energy gained or lost” — no separate bookkeeping needed once you
know the speeds
fields.example: m = 2 kg, u = 3 m/s, v = 7 m/s. Find the net work done?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting W here is the NET work of ALL forces combined, not just one force acting on the
object.
• Forgetting negative work is common (and expected) whenever a force decelerates the object.
• Confusing this with the rotational analogue, which uses ½Iω² instead of $\frac{1}{2}$mv².
fields.conceptual_overview: The Work-Energy Theorem establishes that the total work done by all forces (conservative, non-conservative, internal, and external) acting on a body equals the net change in its translational kinetic energy. It converts force-displacement problems into scalar energy calculations
fields.real_world_applications:
Automotive Crash Safety: Designing front crumple zones to absorb kinetic energy and reduce deceleration impact forces on passengers.

Aircraft Arresting Gear: Sizing hydraulic arrestor cables on aircraft carriers to safely absorb jet kinetic energy during landing
fields.jee_neet_exam_tips:
Applicability: Valid across all reference frames, provided pseudo-force work ($W_{\text{pseudo}}$) is included when using non-inertial frames
.Variable Force Integration: Always apply $\int F(x) \, dx = \Delta K$ when force varies with position.
fields.step_by_step_derivation:
Step 1: Express net force using Newton's Second Law:$$F_{\text{net}} = m a = m \frac{dv}{dt}$$
Step 2: Express differential work $dW$ using chain rule differential $ds = v \, dt$:$$dW = F_{\text{net}} \, ds = \left(m \frac{dv}{dt}\right) ds = m v \, dv$$
Step 3: Integrate differential work from initial speed $u$ to final speed $v$:$$W_{\text{net}} = \int_{u}^{v} m v \, dv = m \left[ \frac{v^2}{2} \right]_{u}^{v}$$
Step 4: Evaluate definite integral bounds:$$W_{\text{net}} = \frac{1}{2} m v^2 - \frac{1}{2} m u^2 = K_f - K_i = \Delta K$$

fields.title: Hooke's Law
fields.variables: F = Restoring force,  k = Spring constant,  x = Displacement from equilibrium
fields.description: The force (F) needed to extend or compress a spring by some distance (x) scales linearly with respect to that distance.
fields.when_to_use: When analyzing springs, elastic materials
fields.mnemonic: “Springs always push back” — the restoring force always opposes the displacement.
fields.example: k = 200 N/m, x = 0.05 m (stretched). Find F?
fields.answer: F = −200×0.05 = −10 N (a 10 N restoring force, opposing the stretch)
fields.common_mistakes:
• Dropping the negative sign, which represents the restoring nature of the force — that's the
whole physical point of the law.
• Assuming k is identical for stretching and compressing — real springs can behave slightly
differently at extremes.
• Forgetting Hooke's law only holds within the elastic limit — beyond that, F is no longer
proportional to x.
fields.conceptual_overview: Hooke's Law states that within the elastic limit of a material, the restoring force ($F$) exerted by an ideal elastic spring is directly proportional to the displacement ($x$) from its natural equilibrium length. The negative sign signifies that restoring forces oppose displacement
fields.real_world_applications:
Structural Strain Gauges: Measuring mechanical strain and load distribution across bridge girders.

Vehicle Suspension Systems: Designing helical shock absorber springs tailored to vehicle mass profiles
fields.jee_neet_exam_tips:
Spring Combinations:Series Connection: $\frac{1}{k_{\text{eq}}} = \frac{1}{k_1} + \frac{1}{k_2}$
Parallel Connection: $k_{\text{eq}} = k_1 + k_2$Cutting Springs: Cutting a spring of constant $k$ into $N$ equal parts increases each segment's spring constant to $N \cdot k$.
fields.step_by_step_derivation:
Step 1: Express linear elasticity proportionality for small displacement $x$:$$F \propto -x$$
Step 2: Introduce spring constant $k$ (stiffness measure):$$F = -kx$$
Step 3: Derive elastic potential energy ($U$) by integrating work done against restoring force:$$U = -\int_{0}^{x} (-kx) \, dx = \int_{0}^{x} kx \, dx$$
Step 4: Evaluate integral:$$U = \frac{1}{2} k x^2$$

fields.title: Gravitational Potential Energy
fields.variables: U = Gravitational potential energy,  G = Universal gravitational constant,  M ,m = Interacting masses,  r = Distance between masses
fields.description: The potential energy(U) an object with mass(m) has due to the gravitational potential of its position(r) in a gravitational field(G)
fields.when_to_use: When calculating escape energies, orbital energy budgets or energy changes as object moves within gravitational field
fields.given_by: calculating the work needed to bring a mass from infinity — where gravity's pull is considered zero — into the grip of another body's gravitational field, treating infinite separation as the natural zero point of reference
fields.mnemonic:
“Always negative, always bound” — the minus sign shows the two masses attract, with U rising
(less negative) as they separate.
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting the negative sign — dropping it reverses the physical meaning entirely.
• Confusing this with the local approximation U = mgh, only valid near a planet's surface for small heights.
• Using weight instead of mass m in the formula.
fields.conceptual_overview: Gravitational Potential Energy ($U$) between two point masses ($M$ and $m$) measures the work performed by external agents to assemble the system from infinite separation to distance $r$. The zero reference potential is set at infinity, yielding negative values for all finite separation distances
fields.real_world_applications:
Orbital Insertion Mechanics: Computing escape velocity ($v_e$) and rocket burn durations for satellite insertion into stable orbits.
Interplanetary Gravity Assist Trajectories: Planning gravitational slingshot maneuvers for outer solar system space probes
fields.jee_neet_exam_tips:
Escape Velocity Formula:$$v_e = \sqrt{\frac{2GM}{R}} = \sqrt{2gR} \quad (\approx 11.2 \text{ km/s for Earth})$$
Orbital Speed Relation: $v_e = \sqrt{2} \cdot v_o$, where $v_o = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}}$ is circular orbital speed.
fields.step_by_step_derivation:
Step 1: Write attractive Newton's gravitational force at position $x$:$$F(x) = -\frac{G M m}{x^2}$$
Step 2: Express work done bringing mass $m$ from infinity to distance $r$:$$U(r) = \int_{\infty}^{r} -F(x) \, dx = \int_{\infty}^{r} \frac{G M m}{x^2} \, dx$$
Step 3: Evaluate definite integral:$$U(r) = G M m \left[ -\frac{1}{x} \right]_{\infty}^{r} = G M m \left( -\frac{1}{r} - 0 \right)$$
Step 4: Simplify to isolate scalar potential energy:$$U = -\frac{GMm}{r}$$

fields.title: Banking of Roads
fields.variables: θ = Angle of banking,  v = Velocity of vehicle,  r = Radius of curve,  g = Acceleration due to gravity
fields.description: The practice of raising the outer edge of a curved road surface at a specific angle relative to the horizontal.
fields.when_to_use: When designing highways, racetracks or railway tracks
fields.given_by: tilting the road surface itself so that a component of the normal force supplies the centripetal pull needed for circular motion, easing the burden that friction alone would otherwise have to carry
fields.mnemonic: “Faster turn, steeper tilt” — the ideal banking angle grows with the square of speed.
fields.example: v = 20 m/s, r = 100 m, g = 10 m/s². Find θ?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting this is the ideal banking angle assuming NO friction is needed — real roads combine
banking with friction, allowing a range of safe speeds.
• Using an arbitrary speed instead of the specific design speed the road was banked for.
• Confusing r (radius of the curve) with the road's width or a car's steering radius.
fields.conceptual_overview: Road banking involves raising the outer edge of a curved roadway relative to its inner edge at an angle $\theta$. Tilting the surface directs a component of the normal contact force inward toward the center of curvature, supplying required centripetal acceleration without depending on tire-road friction
fields.real_world_applications:
High-Speed Rail Track Design: Calculating super-elevation height on curved rail lines to prevent train derailments.
NASCAR Track Construction: Engineering steep high-speed banked turns (up to $31^\circ$ at Daytona)
fields.jee_neet_exam_tips: Optimum Safe Speed (Zero Friction):$$v_{\text{opt}} = \sqrt{rg \tan\theta}$$Maximum Speed with Friction Coefficient $\mu$:$$v_{\max} = \sqrt{rg \left( \frac{\mu + \tan\theta}{1 - \mu \tan\theta} \right)}$$
fields.step_by_step_derivation:
Step 1: Resolve normal force $N$ on banked incline $\theta$ into vertical and horizontal components:$$N_{\text{vertical}} = N \cos\theta, \quad N_{\text{horizontal}} = N \sin\theta$$
Step 2: Balance vertical forces for zero vertical acceleration:$$N \cos\theta = mg$$
Step 3: Equate horizontal component to required centripetal force:$$N \sin\theta = \frac{m v^2}{r}$$
Step 4: Divide horizontal equation by vertical equation:$$\frac{N \sin\theta}{N \cos\theta} = \frac{\frac{m v^2}{r}}{mg} \implies \tan\theta = \frac{v^2}{rg}$$

fields.title: Moment of Inertia (Rod)
fields.variables: I = Moment of inertia,  M = Mass of rod,  L = Length of rod
fields.description: It is  measure of an object's resistance(I) to changes in its rotational motion, depending on both its mass(M) and how that mass is distributed relative to the axis of rotation(L)
fields.when_to_use: When modelling rotation of rods, beams
fields.given_by: integrating the mass distributed along a thin rod's length, where each tiny element's contribution to rotational inertia grows with the square of its distance from the rod's midpoint
fields.mnemonic:
“Centre axis keeps I small” — rotating about the middle, mass stays close to the axis on both
sides.
fields.example: M = 1.5 kg, L = 2 m, rotation about the centre. Find I?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting this is specifically for rotation about the CENTRE — rotating about one END instead
uses I = $\frac{1}{3}$ML² (four times larger).
• Confusing L (rod length) with R (used in disk/sphere formulas) — a rod problem has no radius
 here.
• Assuming this applies to a thick or non-uniform rod — it assumes a thin, uniform one.
fields.conceptual_overview: The Moment of Inertia ($I$) quantifies a rigid body's rotational inertia about a specified axis. For a thin, uniform rod of total mass $M$ and length $L$, the moment of inertia about an axis passing through its center of mass perpendicular to its length evaluates mass distribution about its center
fields.real_world_applications:
Helicopter Main Rotor Dynamics: Calculating rotational inertia for rotor blade power requirements.

Robotic Manipulator Arm Controls: Sizing motor torque outputs based on joint arm segment inertia
fields.jee_neet_exam_tips: Axis Through One End: Applying the Parallel Axis Theorem ($I = I_{\text{cm}} + M d^2$ with $d = \frac{L}{2}$):$$I_{\text{end}} = \frac{1}{12} M L^2 + M \left(\frac{L}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{3} M L^2$$
fields.step_by_step_derivation:
Step 1: Define linear mass density: $\lambda = \frac{M}{L}$
Step 2: Choose differential element $dx$ at distance $x$ from central axis with mass $dm = \lambda \, dx = \left(\frac{M}{L}\right) dx$
Step 3: Express differential moment of inertia:$$dI = dm \cdot x^2 = \left(\frac{M}{L}\right) x^2 \, dx$$
Step 4: Integrate across length limits from $x = -\frac{L}{2}$ to $x = +\frac{L}{2}$:$$I = \frac{M}{L} \int_{-L/2}^{L/2} x^2 \, dx = \frac{M}{L} \left[ \frac{x^3}{3} \right]_{-L/2}^{L/2} = \frac{M}{3L} \left( \frac{L^3}{8} - \left(-\frac{L^3}{8}\right) \right) = \frac{1}{12} M L^2$$

fields.title: Moment of Inertia (disk)
fields.variables: I = Moment of inertia,  M = Mass of disk,  R = Radius of disk
fields.description: The measure of an object's resistance(I) to changes in its rotational motion, depending on both its mass and how that mass is distributed relative to the axis of rotation(R)
fields.when_to_use: When analyzing rotating wheels, disks or pulleys
fields.given_by: integrating over concentric rings of mass spread across a flat circular disk, each ring resisting rotation in proportion to how far it sits from the axis running through the center
fields.mnemonic:
“A disk splits the difference” — its coefficient (½) sits between a thin rod about its centre (1/12)
and a hoop (1).
fields.example: M = 3 kg, R = 0.2 m. Find I?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Confusing a solid disk ($\frac{1}{2}$MR²) with a thin ring/hoop (MR², no fraction) — the disk's mass fills the
whole face, the hoop's sits only at the rim.
• Forgetting this is I about the axis through the centre, perpendicular to the disk's face — rotating
about a diameter instead gives $\frac{1}{4}$MR².
• Using diameter instead of radius R.
fields.conceptual_overview: The moment of inertia of a thin, flat, uniform circular disk of mass $M$ and radius $R$ about a central axis perpendicular to its face measures 2D planar mass distribution. It forms the baseline model for rotating solid circular structures
fields.real_world_applications:
Energy Storage Flywheels: Maximizing stored rotational kinetic energy in industrial flywheels.

Vehicular Disc Brake Design: Analyzing rotational momentum during heavy braking operations.
fields.jee_neet_exam_tips: Diameter Axis Shortcut: Applying the Perpendicular Axis Theorem ($I_z = I_x + I_y \implies \frac{1}{2}MR^2 = 2 I_{\text{dia}}$):$$I_{\text{diameter}} = \frac{1}{4} M R^2$$
fields.step_by_step_derivation:
Step 1: Define surface mass density: $\sigma = \frac{M}{\pi R^2}$
Step 2: Select thin concentric ring element of radius $r$ and width $dr$. Ring area $dA = 2\pi r \, dr$, mass $dm = \sigma \, dA = \left(\frac{M}{\pi R^2}\right) 2\pi r \, dr = \frac{2M}{R^2} r \, dr$
Step 3: Express differential moment of inertia $dI$ for ring element:$$dI = dm \cdot r^2 = \frac{2M}{R^2} r^3 \, dr$$Step 4: Integrate from $r = 0$ to $r = R$:$$I = \frac{2M}{R^2} \int_{0}^{R} r^3 \, dr = \frac{2M}{R^2} \left[ \frac{r^4}{4} \right]_{0}^{R} = \frac{1}{2} M R^2$$

fields.title: Moment of Inertia (sphere)
fields.variables: I = Moment of inertia,  M = Mass of sphere,  R = Radius of sphere
fields.description: The  measure of an object's resistance to changes in its rotational motion(I), depending on both its mass(M) and how that mass is distributed relative to the axis of rotation(R)
fields.when_to_use: When computing rotational dynamics of spherical bodies such as balls, planets
fields.given_by: integrating the mass of infinitesimally thin disks stacked through a solid sphere, each contributing its own resistance to rotation about the central axis, then summing their effects across the entire volume
fields.mnemonic:
“Mass spread through the whole volume, not just the rim” — a solid sphere's coefficient (2/5) is
smaller than a hollow shell's (2/3).
fields.example: M = 2 kg, R = 0.1 m. Find I?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Confusing a solid sphere ($\frac{2}{5}$ MR²) with a hollow spherical shell ($\frac{2}{3}$ MR²) — easy to mix up
under pressure.
• Forgetting R is measured from the sphere's centre to its surface.
• Forgetting this formula assumes uniform density throughout the sphere.
fields.conceptual_overview: For a uniform solid sphere of mass $M$ and radius $R$, the moment of inertia about any axis passing through its central diameter reflects its 3D mass distribution. Being concentrated closer to the axis of rotation compared to a hollow shell, a solid sphere exhibits lower rotational resistance
fields.real_world_applications:
Precision Gyroscope Design: Calibration of inertial navigation gyroscopes for aerospace positioning.

Ball Bearing Mechanical Optimization: Calculating angular momentum losses in spherical steel bearings
fields.jee_neet_exam_tips:
Solid vs. Thin Spherical Shell Comparison:Solid Sphere: $I = \frac{2}{5} M R^2 = 0.4 M R^2$Hollow Sphere: $I = \frac{2}{3} M R^2 \approx 0.67 M R^2$
Inclined Plane Rolling Speed: A solid sphere wins rolling races down inclines against disks, rings, and hollow spheres due to its lower $\frac{I}{MR^2}$ ratio
fields.step_by_step_derivation:
Step 1: Define volumetric mass density: $\rho = \frac{M}{\frac{4}{3}\pi R^3} = \frac{3M}{4\pi R^3}$
Step 2: Divide sphere into elemental coaxial disks of radius $r = \sqrt{R^2 - z^2}$ and thickness $dz$ at height $z$. Disk mass $dm = \rho (\pi r^2) dz = \rho \pi (R^2 - z^2) dz$
Step 3: Differential moment of inertia for elemental disk ($dI = \frac{1}{2} dm \cdot r^2$):$$dI = \frac{1}{2} [\rho \pi (R^2 - z^2) dz] (R^2 - z^2) = \frac{1}{2} \rho \pi (R^2 - z^2)^2 dz$$
Step 4: Integrate from $z = -R$ to $z = +R$:$$I = \frac{1}{2} \pi \rho \int_{-R}^{R} (R^4 - 2R^2 z^2 + z^4) \, dz = \frac{2}{5} M R^2$$

fields.title: Rotational Kinetic Energy
fields.variables: KE = Rotational kinetic energy,  I = Moment of inertia,  ω = Angular velocity
fields.description: The energy(KE) an object possesses due to its rotation around an axis, determined by its moment of inertia(I) and angular velocity(Ω)
fields.when_to_use: When calculating energy stored in spinning flywheels, rolling objects or rotating machineries
fields.given_by: treating a spinning rigid body as a collection of countless tiny masses, each tracing its own circle at its own speed, and summing up the kinetic energy each carries — but expressed through the single, elegant language of angular velocity
fields.mnemonic: “Same shape as linear KE, but I replaces m and ω replaces v.”
fields.example: I = 4 kg·m², ω = 3 rad/s. Find KE?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting ω must be in rad/s, not rpm or Hz, before plugging in.
• Forgetting a rolling object has BOTH translational and rotational KE: total = $\frac{1}{2}$mv² + $\frac{1}{2}$Iω².
• Using linear velocity v in place of ω by mistake.
fields.conceptual_overview: Rotational Kinetic Energy ($K_{\text{rot}}$) represents energy stored in a body due to its angular velocity ($\omega$) about an axis of rotation. It serves as the rotational analogue to linear translational kinetic energy ($\frac{1}{2}mv^2$), using moment of inertia ($I$) in place of inertial mass ($m$)
fields.real_world_applications:
Grid Energy Storage Flywheels: Storing surplus renewable electrical energy as mechanical rotational kinetic energy.

Turbine Rotor Balancing: Estimating dynamic operational energy stored in spinning steam/gas power turbines
fields.jee_neet_exam_tips:
Total Kinetic Energy of Rolling Without Slipping ($v = R\omega$):$$K_{\text{total}} = K_{\text{trans}} + K_{\text{rot}} = \frac{1}{2} m v^2 \left( 1 + \frac{k^2}{R^2} \right)$$(where $k$ is the radius of gyration)
Angular Momentum Equivalence:$$K_{\text{rot}} = \frac{L^2}{2I} \quad (\text{analogous to } K = \frac{p^2}{2m})$$
fields.step_by_step_derivation:
Step 1: Consider a rigid body rotating at angular speed $\omega$, composed of discrete particles $m_i$ at radial distances $r_i$ with linear speeds $v_i = r_i \omega$
Step 2: Sum translational kinetic energy across all constituent particles:$$K_{\text{rot}} = \sum \frac{1}{2} m_i v_i^2 = \sum \frac{1}{2} m_i (r_i \omega)^2$$
Step 3: Factor out constant term $\frac{1}{2} \omega^2$:$$K_{\text{rot}} = \frac{1}{2} \left( \sum m_i r_i^2 \right) \omega^2$$
Step 4: Substitute definition of Moment of Inertia ($I = \sum m_i r_i^2$):$$K_{\text{rot}} = \frac{1}{2} I \omega^2$$

fields.title: Parallel Axis Theorem
fields.variables: I = Moment of inertia,  I_c = Moment of inertia about center of mass,  M = Mass,  d = Perpendicular distance
fields.description: The parallel axis theorem allows calculation of a body's moment of inertia about any axis parallel to one through its center of mass by adding the product of its mass and the square of the distance.
fields.when_to_use: When axis of rotation does not pass through object's center, such as pendulum swinging from a pivot at its edge
fields.mnemonic: “Centre of mass first, then pay a penalty for moving the axis” — you always add, never subtract.
fields.example:
A rod has $I_c$= $\frac{1}{12}$ML² about its centre.
 Find I about one end (d = $\frac{L}{2}$)?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting $I_c$ must specifically be about an axis through the centre of mass — this theorem
doesn't connect two arbitrary parallel axes.
• Forgetting d is the perpendicular distance between the two parallel axes.
• Forgetting I about any shifted axis is always ≥ $I_c$, never smaller.
fields.conceptual_overview: The Parallel Axis Theorem allows calculation of the moment of inertia ($I$) of any rigid body about an arbitrary axis, provided the moment of inertia about a parallel axis passing through its center of mass ($I_{\text{cm}}$), total body mass ($M$), and perpendicular distance ($d$) between the two axes are known
fields.real_world_applications:
Connecting Rod Balancing: Calculating rotational inertia of engine components about crankpin pivot journals.

Pendulum Clock Calibration: Adjusting pendulum bob heights to fine-tune system oscillation periods
fields.jee_neet_exam_tips:
Center of Mass Requirement: $I_{\text{cm}}$ must be the axis passing strictly through the body's center of mass.
3D Plane Validity: Unlike the Perpendicular Axis Theorem (which is restricted to 2D planar lamina), the Parallel Axis Theorem is valid for all 3D rigid bodies
fields.step_by_step_derivation:
Step 1: Choose center of mass as origin. Consider particle $m_i$ at $(x_i, y_i)$. Parallel axis $Z'$ passes through $(d, 0)$.
Step 2: Express distance squared $r_i'^2$ of particle $m_i$ from $Z'$ axis:$$r_i'^2 = (x_i - d)^2 + y_i^2 = x_i^2 - 2 x_i d + d^2 + y_i^2 = (x_i^2 + y_i^2) - 2 x_i d + d^2$$
Step 3: Sum over all particles to find moment of inertia $I = \sum m_i r_i'^2$:$$I = \sum m_i (x_i^2 + y_i^2) - 2 d \sum m_i x_i + d^2 \sum m_i$$
Step 4: By definition of center of mass origin, $\sum m_i x_i = 0$, $\sum m_i = M$, and $\sum m_i (x_i^2 + y_i^2) = I_{\text{cm}}$:$$I = I_{\text{cm}} + M d^2$$

fields.title: Angular Impulse
fields.variables: J = Angular impulse,  τ = Applied torque,  Δt = Time interval, ΔL = Chnage in angular momentum
fields.description: It quantifies the effect of torque(τ) over a period of  time(t)
fields.when_to_use: When analyzing sudden rotational impact, such as cue striking or billiard ball
fields.given_by: extending the idea of linear impulse into rotational motion — considering how a torque, sustained over an interval of time, doesn't just act in an instant but accumulates to change how fast something spins
fields.mnemonic:
“Torque held over time changes spin” — the rotational twin of the linear impulse-momentum
theorem.
fields.example: τ = 5 N·m applied for Δt = 2 s. Find ΔL?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Confusing this rotational impulse with ordinary linear impulse (J = FΔt = Δp) — same structure,
different quantities.
• Forgetting τ must be constant (or an average value) over the interval for this simple form to
apply directly.
• Forgetting angular momentum L, like linear momentum, is a vector — direction matters.
fields.conceptual_overview: Angular Impulse ($J_\theta$) quantifies the cumulative rotational effect of a torque ($\tau$) applied over a time duration $\Delta t$. Analogous to linear momentum impulse ($F \Delta t = \Delta p$), an applied angular impulse produces an exact, equal change in the system's angular momentum ($\Delta L$)
fields.real_world_applications:
Clutch Engagement Systems: Calculating transient slip torque pulses required to match engine shaft speeds with vehicle transmissions.

Spacecraft Thruster Stabilization: Delivering brief reaction control torque pulses to adjust satellite angular orientations
fields.jee_neet_exam_tips:
Area Under Curve: On a Torque vs. Time ($\tau \text{ vs } t$) graph, the net area under the curve equals total angular impulse ($J_\theta = \Delta L$).
Collisional Angular Conservation: When impulsive forces act through a pivot point ($\vec{r} = 0$), net angular impulse about that pivot is zero, conserving angular momentum $\vec{L}$.
fields.step_by_step_derivation:
Step 1: Express rotational form of Newton's Second Law:$$\vec{\tau} = \frac{d\vec{L}}{dt}$$
Step 2: Separate differential variables:$$d\vec{L} = \vec{\tau} \, dt$$
Step 3: Integrate across time duration $t_1 \to t_2$:$$\vec{J}_\theta = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} \vec{\tau} \, dt = \int_{L_1}^{L_2} d\vec{L} = \vec{L}_2 - \vec{L}_1 = \Delta \vec{L}$$
Step 4: For constant torque applied over time interval $\Delta t$:$$J_\theta = \tau \Delta t = \Delta L = I \omega_f - I \omega_i$$

fields.title: First Law of Thermodynamics
fields.variables: dU = Change in internal energy of a system,  dQ = Total heat supplied,  dW = Total work done by the system
fields.description: The Change in Internal Energy(U) of a system is difference of Heat supplied(Q) and Work done(W) by the system.
fields.when_to_use: When tracking energy balance in engines, refrigeration processes
fields.mnemonic:
“What you gain, minus what you spend, stays inside” — internal energy change equals heat
added minus work done BY the system.
fields.example: A gas absorbs 500 J of heat and does 200 J of work on its surroundings. Find dU?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Mixing up sign conventions — some textbooks define dW as work done ON the system (dU = dQ
+ dW instead), so always check which convention is in use.
• Forgetting Q and W are path-dependent (they depend on the specific process), while U itself is
 a state function.
• Assuming dU = 0 automatically unless the problem explicitly states an isothermal ideal-gas
process.
fields.conceptual_overview: The First Law of Thermodynamics states the Law of Conservation of Energy for thermodynamic systems. It establishes that net heat added to a system ($dQ$) equals the increase in its internal energy ($dU$) plus external work performed by the system ($dW$)
fields.real_world_applications:
Internal Combustion Engines: Calculating thermal efficiency by comparing fuel combustion heat input ($dQ$) against piston output work ($dW$).
Refrigeration & Heat Pumps: Engineering closed-loop compressor work cycles to transfer heat out of cold compartments.
fields.jee_neet_exam_tips:
Standard Sign Conventions:$dQ > 0$: Heat added to system; $dQ < 0$: Heat extracted from system.$dW > 0$: 
Work done by system (expansion); $dW < 0$: Work done on system (compression).State Function vs. Path Function: $U$ is a state function ($\oint dU = 0$ over any closed cycle), whereas $Q$ and $W$ are path functions.
fields.step_by_step_derivation:
Step 1: State conservation of total system energy ($E_{\text{in}} = E_{\text{out}} + \Delta E_{\text{system}}$)
Step 2: Express differential heat added ($dQ$) and differential work performed ($dW$):$$dQ = dU + dW$$
Step 3: Rearrange to isolate differential internal energy change ($dU$):$$dU = dQ - dW$$
Step 4: Substitute mechanical boundary expansion work $dW = P \, dV$:$$dU = dQ - P \, dV$$

fields.title: Boyle's Law
fields.variables: P1,P2 = Initial and final pressures,  V1,V2 = Initial and final volumes
fields.description: Describes the relationship between the pressure(P) and volume(V) of a gas at constant temperature.
fields.when_to_use: When analyzing isothermal compression or expansion of gas, such as in springes or diving cyclinders
fields.mnemonic:
“Squeeze the volume, pressure pushes back harder” — an inverse relationship at constant
temperature.
fields.example:
P
1
 = 100 kPa, V1
 = 4 L. Find P2
 when V2
 = 2 L.
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting this only holds at constant temperature — heating or cooling during compression
breaks the relationship.
• Treating P and V as directly proportional instead of inversely proportional.
• Mixing this up with Charles's law, which relates V and T rather than P and V.
fields.conceptual_overview: Boyle's Law states that the absolute pressure ($P$) exerted by a given mass of an ideal gas is inversely proportional to the volume ($V$) it occupies, provided system temperature ($T$) remains constant (isothermal process)
fields.real_world_applications:
Scuba Diving Respiration: Calculating expanding air volume in diver lungs during ascent to prevent pulmonary barotrauma.

Pneumatic Reciprocating Compressors: Designing mechanical piston displacements to compress industrial air volumes
fields.jee_neet_exam_tips:
Isothermal Work Done:$$W = n R T \ln\left(\frac{V_2}{V_1}\right) = 2.303 n R T \log_{10}\left(\frac{P_1}{P_2}\right)$$
Internal Energy Change: For an ideal gas in an isothermal process ($\Delta T = 0$), internal energy change is zero ($\Delta U = 0$).
fields.step_by_step_derivation:
Step 1: Express Ideal Gas Law ($P V = n R T$).
Step 2: For an isothermal process ($T = \text{constant}$) with fixed gas quantity ($n = \text{constant}$):$$P V = \text{constant}$$
Step 3: Equate initial state 1 to final state 2 along an isothermal curve:$$P_1 V_1 = P_2 V_2$$

fields.title: Charle's Law
fields.variables: V1,V2 = Initial volumes,  T1,T2 = Initial temperature
fields.description: Explains how gases expand or contract upon heating
fields.when_to_use: When scaling thermal expansion boundaries for hot-air baloons, gas cylinders
fields.mnemonic:
“Volume and temperature rise together” — at constant pressure, gas expands proportionally with
absolute temperature.
fields.example:
V1
= 2 L at T1
 = 300 K. Find V2
 at T2
 = 450 K.
fields.common_mistakes:
• Using Celsius instead of Kelvin — this ratio only holds with absolute temperature.
• Forgetting this assumes constant pressure — if pressure also changes, the combined gas law is
 needed instead.
• Confusing this with Gay-Lussac's law ($\frac{P}{T}$ = constant at fixed volume), which tracks pressure
instead of volume.
fields.conceptual_overview: Charles's Law states that the volume ($V$) of a fixed mass of an ideal gas is directly proportional to its absolute temperature ($T$ in Kelvin), provided system pressure ($P$) remains strictly constant. As thermal energy increases, molecular speeds rise, expanding gas volume to maintain constant wall impact pressure
fields.real_world_applications:
Hot Air Balloon Flight: Heating air inside balloon envelopes expands gas volume, displacing cooler ambient air to generate buoyant lift.

Gas Thermometer Design: Measuring absolute cryogenic temperatures through proportional gas volume displacement at constant pressure
fields.jee_neet_exam_tips:
Absolute Temperature Requirement: Temperature $T$ must always be expressed in Kelvin ($K = ^\circ\text{C} + 273.15$).
Isobaric Work Done:$$W = P \Delta V = n R \Delta T$$
fields.step_by_step_derivation:
Step 1: Start with Ideal Gas Equation ($P V = n R T$).
Step 2: Isolate ratio of volume to temperature under constant pressure ($P$) and mole count ($n$):$$\frac{V}{T} = \frac{n R}{P} = \text{constant}$$
Step 3: Relate two distinct thermodynamic states along an isobaric path ($1 \to 2$):$$\frac{V_1}{T_1} = \frac{V_2}{T_2}$$

fields.title: Mean Free Path
fields.variables: λ = Mean free path,  n = Number density,  d = Diameter of gas molecule
fields.description: The average distance a particle travels between collisions in a gas, and it is influenced by factors such as particle density and size.
fields.when_to_use: When configuring vaccum chambers, tracing microscopic diffusion barriers
fields.mnemonic: “Bigger molecules, more crowding, shorter free path” — λ shrinks as either n or d grows.
fields.common_mistakes:
• Dropping the √2 factor, which accounts for the fact that all molecules are moving, not just the
one you're tracking.
• Confusing number density n (molecules per m³) with moles or mass density.
• Using molecular radius instead of molecular diameter d.
fields.conceptual_overview: Mean Free Path ($\lambda$) represents the average distance traveled by a moving gas molecule between successive elastic collisions with other molecules. It characterizes transport processes like diffusion, viscosity, and thermal conductivity in kinetic gas theory
fields.real_world_applications:
Vacuum Chamber Engineering: Achieving ultra-high vacuum levels so mean free path exceeds chamber dimensions, enabling thin-film semiconductor deposition.

Atmospheric Re-entry Aerodynamics: Modeling rarefied gas dynamics around high-altitude spacecraft
fields.jee_neet_exam_tips:
Pressure & Temperature Dependence (Ideal Gas $P = n k_B T$):$$\lambda = \frac{k_B T}{\sqrt{2} \pi d^2 P} \implies \lambda \propto \frac{T}{P}$$
Constant Volume Scaling: If volume $V$ and mass are fixed ($n = \text{constant}$), mean free path $\lambda$ remains unchanged despite temperature variations.
fields.step_by_step_derivation:
Step 1: Model a target molecule of effective collision diameter $d$ moving at average speed $v$. It collides with any molecule whose center lies within collision cross-section $\sigma = \pi d^2$.
Step 2: Volume swept out in time $t$: $V_{\text{swept}} = (\pi d^2) v t$
Step 3: Collision count $N_c$ in molecular number density $n = \frac{N}{V}$: $N_c = n \pi d^2 v t$.
Step 4: Calculate average distance between collisions ($\lambda = \frac{v t}{N_c}$):$$\lambda_{\text{simple}} = \frac{1}{n \pi d^2}$$
Step 5: Apply Maxwellian relative velocity correction factor ($\sqrt{2}$) for randomly moving gas molecules:$$\lambda = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2} n \pi d^2}$$

fields.title: Specific Heat Capacity
fields.variables: Q = Transferred heat energy,  m = Mass of substance,  c = Specific heat capacity,  T = Temperature
fields.description: Amount of heat(Q) required to raise the temperature(T) of a unit mass of a substance by one degree Celsius or one Kelvin.
fields.when_to_use: When managing phase boundaries, cooling calculations or balancing industrial caloric exchangers
fields.given_by: the total thermal energy required to change the temperature of a distinct mass of a substance
fields.mnemonic: “More mass, bigger temperature swing, more heat needed” — a simple triple product.
fields.example: m = 2 kg water, c = 4200 J/(kg·K), ΔT = 20 K. Find Q?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Reusing water's c value for a different material — c is specific to each substance.
• Forgetting ΔT is a temperature CHANGE, not an absolute temperature.
• Applying this formula across a phase change (melting/boiling) — that needs latent heat instead,
since temperature stays constant during the phase change.
fields.conceptual_overview: Specific Heat Capacity ($c$) defines the quantity of thermal energy ($Q$) required to raise the temperature of a unit mass ($m$) of a substance by one degree Celsius (or Kelvin). It measures a material's intrinsic thermal inertia
fields.real_world_applications:
Automotive Engine Coolants: Utilizing water's exceptionally high specific heat capacity ($c \approx 4184 \text{ J/kg}\cdot\text{K}$) to absorb combustion heat effectively.
Thermal Energy Storage: Selecting phase-change and high specific heat materials for solar thermal energy storage systems
fields.jee_neet_exam_tips:
Molar Heat Capacity Relation:$$C_m = M \cdot c \quad (M = \text{molar mass})$$
Water Thermal Calibrations: $c_{\text{water}} = 1 \text{ cal/g}^\circ\text{C} = 4.184 \text{ J/g}^\circ\text{C}$; $c_{\text{ice}} \approx 0.5 \text{ cal/g}^\circ\text{C}$.
fields.step_by_step_derivation:
Step 1: Define heat capacity $C$ as thermal energy added per temperature change:$$C = \frac{dQ}{dT}$$
Step 2: Normalize heat capacity per unit mass to obtain specific heat capacity $c$:$$c = \frac{1}{m} \frac{dQ}{dT} \implies dQ = m c \, dT$$
Step 3: Integrate for constant specific heat $c$ over finite temperature change $\Delta T = T_f - T_i$:$$Q = m c \Delta T$$

fields.title: Newton's Law of Cooling
fields.variables: dT/dt = Rate of temperature drop over time,  k = Thermal cooling proportionality constant,  T = Instantaneous body temperature,  T_0 = Surrounding environment temperature
fields.description: The rate at which an object loses heat is proportional to the difference between its temperature(T) and the ambient temperature(T_0)
fields.when_to_use: To model atmospheric temperature decay curves or engineer passive safe cooldown timers for hot mechanical processes
fields.mnemonic:
“Hotter than the room, faster it cools” — the rate of cooling is proportional to how far above the
surroundings the object is.
fields.example: $T_{0}$ = 25°C (room), k = 0.05 /min, current T = 80°C. Find the instantaneous cooling rate?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting this is only a good approximation for small temperature differences — it isn't exact
at every ΔT.
• Missing that the negative sign just means T moves toward $T_0$, whichever direction that is(cooling if T>$T_0$, warming if T<$T_0$).
• Confusing this instantaneous-rate equation with its solved form T(t) = $T_0$+(Ti−T0)$e^{-kt}$, which
requires integrating it.
fields.conceptual_overview: Newton's Law of Cooling states that the rate of heat loss of a body by radiation and natural convection is directly proportional to the temperature difference between the body ($T$) and its surrounding environment ($T_0$), provided this temperature difference remains small
fields.real_world_applications:
Forensic Pathology: Estimating time of death (algor mortis) by measuring body core temperature relative to ambient air.

Industrial Metal Heat Treatment: Controlling cooling rates during quenching processes to achieve targeted steel grain structures
fields.jee_neet_exam_tips:
Approximate Average Form for Rapid Numerical Calculations:$$\frac{T_1 - T_2}{t} = k \left( \frac{T_1 + T_2}{2} - T_0 \right)$$
Validity Limit: Accurate primarily when temperature differences are modest ($\Delta T < 30^\circ\text{C}$). 
For large differences, apply Stefan-Boltzmann radiation ($T^4$).
fields.step_by_step_derivation:
Step 1: Express rate of temperature change proportionality:$$\frac{dT}{dt} \propto -(T - T_0)$$
Step 2: Introduce cooling constant $k$:$$\frac{dT}{dt} = -k(T - T_0)$$
Step 3: Separate variables and integrate from initial temperature $T_i$ at $t=0$ to $T(t)$:$$\int_{T_i}^{T} \frac{dT}{T - T_0} = -k \int_{0}^{t} dt \implies \ln\left(\frac{T - T_0}{T_i - T_0}\right) = -k t$$

fields.title: Capacitors in Series
fields.variables: 1/C = Total capacitance,  1/C1, 1,C2 = Individual capacitances
fields.description: When capacitors are connected in series, the total capacitance is less than the smallest individual capacitor, and all capacitors carry the same charge while the voltage divides among them.
fields.when_to_use: When distributing a high operating voltage evenly across lower-rated storage components to safeguard circuitry fields
fields.given_by: the fact that capacitors in series carry the same charge, while the total voltage splits across each — the reciprocals of capacitance add, similar in form to resistors in parallel
fields.mnemonic:
“Series capacitors always end up weaker than the weakest one” — like parallel resistors, but for
capacitance
fields.example:
C1
= 2 μF, C2
= 3 μF. Find C?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting to take the reciprocal at the end to recover C, not $\frac{1}{C}$.
• Forgetting series capacitance is always smaller than the smallest individual capacitor — a good
 sanity check.
• Mixing this up with the parallel capacitor formula, which simply adds values directly.
fields.conceptual_overview: When capacitors are connected in series, electrostatic induction forces each capacitor to store the exact same magnitude of charge ($Q$). Total applied voltage splits across components inversely proportional to their individual capacitances, reducing overall equivalent capacitance below that of any individual capacitor
fields.real_world_applications:
High-Voltage Stacks: Connecting lower-voltage rated capacitors in series to withstand high operating voltages without dielectric breakdown.

Capacitive Voltage Dividers: Stepping down high-voltage AC lines for high-frequency signal measurement
fields.jee_neet_exam_tips:
Two Capacitors Series Shortcut:$$C_{\text{eq}} = \frac{C_1 C_2}{C_1 + C_2}$$
Charge Equivalence: In an uncharged series chain connected to a battery, every capacitor holds identical charge ($Q_1 = Q_2 = Q_{\text{eq}}$).
fields.step_by_step_derivation:
Step 1: Express total potential drop across series chain:$$V_{\text{total}} = V_1 + V_2 + V_3 + \dots$$
Step 2: Express component voltage drops ($V_k = \frac{Q}{C_k}$):$$V_{\text{total}} = \frac{Q}{C_1} + \frac{Q}{C_2} + \frac{Q}{C_3} + \dots$$
Step 3: Substitute $V_{\text{total}} = \frac{Q}{C_{\text{eq}}}$:$$\frac{Q}{C_{\text{eq}}} = Q \left( \frac{1}{C_1} + \frac{1}{C_2} + \frac{1}{C_3} + \dots \right)$$
Step 4: Divide by common charge $Q$:$$\frac{1}{C_{\text{eq}}} = \frac{1}{C_1} + \frac{1}{C_2} + \frac{1}{C_3} + \dots$$

fields.title: Capacitors in Parallel
fields.variables: C = Total capacitance,  C1,C2,C3 = Individual capacitances
fields.description: If all capacitors are connected in parallel then there sum gives us the total capacitance(
fields.when_to_use: To maximize overall static charge accumulation capacities
fields.given_by: the fact that capacitors in parallel share the same voltage, while total charge is the sum of each — so their capacitances simply add, similar in form to resistors in series
fields.mnemonic:
“Parallel capacitors just add their plate area effectively” — straightforward addition, more
capacitance
fields.example:
C1
 = 2 μF,  C2
= 3 μF,  C3
= 5 μF. Find C?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting parallel capacitors add directly — the opposite behaviour of parallel resistors, which
need reciprocals.
• Mixing this up with the series capacitor formula, which requires reciprocals instead.
• Forgetting all parallel capacitors share the same voltage, while charge divides according to
each capacitor's value.
fields.conceptual_overview: Connecting capacitors in parallel directly increases total charge storage capacity. Because all parallel branches share the same operating voltage ($V$), total stored charge equals the sum of individual charges, behaving as a single equivalent capacitor with a larger effective plate area
fields.real_world_applications:
Power Supply Filtering: Paralleling bulk electrolytic capacitors with high-frequency ceramic capacitors to filter out broad noise spectrums.

Camera Flash Units: Combining parallel capacitor arrays to quickly discharge massive currents into xenon tubes.
fields.jee_neet_exam_tips:
Stored Energy in Parallel Arrays:$$U_{\text{total}} = U_1 + U_2 + \dots = \frac{1}{2} C_{\text{eq}} V^2$$$N$ 
Equal Capacitors ($C$):$$C_{\text{eq}} = N C$$
fields.step_by_step_derivation:
Step 1: Express total stored charge across parallel branches:$$Q_{\text{total}} = Q_1 + Q_2 + Q_3 + \dots$$
Step 2: Express branch charges using fundamental capacitance relation ($Q_k = C_k V$):$$Q_{\text{total}} = C_1 V + C_2 V + C_3 V + \dots$$
Step 3: Substitute $Q_{\text{total}} = C_{\text{eq}} V$:$$C_{\text{eq}} V = V (C_1 + C_2 + C_3 + \dots)$$
Step 4: Divide by common potential difference $V$:$$C_{\text{eq}} = C_1 + C_2 + C_3 + \dots$$

fields.title: Gauss's law
fields.variables: ϕ = Total electric flux,  Q_enc = Total charge enclosed,  ε₀ =   Pemittivity of free space
fields.description: The total electric flux(ϕ) through a closed surface(A) is proportional to the net electric charge(Q) enclosed by that surface.
fields.when_to_use: When deriving field equations for symmetric volumetric objects like charged sphere, coaxial wires
fields.mnemonic:
“Only what's trapped inside the surface counts” — charges outside contribute nothing to the net
flux.
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting Q_enc
 is only the charge inside the Gaussian surface, no matter how close outside
 charges are.
• Choosing a Gaussian surface that doesn't match the symmetry of the charge distribution,
making E hard to isolate from the flux integral.
• Confusing electric flux Φ (field lines through a surface) with the electric field E itself.
fields.conceptual_overview: Gauss's Law states that the total net electric flux ($\Phi_E$) passing outward through any closed hypothetical surface (Gaussian surface) equals the total enclosed electric charge ($Q_{\text{enclosed}}$) divided by the permittivity of free space ($\varepsilon_0$)
fields.real_world_applications:
Faraday Cage Shielding: Designing conductive enclosures that isolate sensitive electronic devices from external electrostatic fields.

Coaxial Cable Design: Calculating radial field distributions and voltage ratings inside shielded transmission cables
fields.jee_neet_exam_tips:
Field Inside Conducting Sphere: Electric field inside a hollow or solid conductor in electrostatic equilibrium is always zero ($\vec{E}_{\text{inside}} = 0$).
Field Near Infinite Sheet of Charge:$$E = \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}$$
fields.step_by_step_derivation:
Step 1: Consider a point charge $q$ enclosed inside a spherical Gaussian surface of radius $r$
Step 2: Write differential electric flux $d\Phi_E$ through area element $d\vec{A}$:$$d\Phi_E = \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{A} = E \, dA \cos(0^\circ) = E \, dA$$
Step 3: Integrate flux across the closed spherical surface area ($A = 4\pi r^2$):$$\Phi_E = \oint E \, dA = E \oint dA = E (4\pi r^2)$$
Step 4: Substitute point charge field magnitude $E = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{q}{r^2}$:$$\Phi_E = \left(\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{q}{r^2}\right) (4\pi r^2) = \frac{q}{\varepsilon_0}$$
Step 5: Generalize for any arbitrary closed surface enclosing net charge $Q_{\text{enclosed}}$:$$\Phi_E = \oint \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{A} = \frac{Q_{\text{enclosed}}}{\varepsilon_0}$$

fields.title: Electric Field (infinite sheet)
fields.variables: E = Electrical field,  σ = Surface charge density per unit area,  ε₀ = Permittivity of free space
fields.description: The electric field is always perpendicular to the surface of the sheet, pointing away from the sheet if the charge is positive and toward the sheet if negative
fields.when_to_use: When tracking field baselines adjacent to massive capacitor plates
fields.mnemonic:
“An infinite sheet's field doesn't care how far you stand” — E stays constant with distance, unlike
a point charge's field.
fields.worked_example:
• Forgetting series resistance is always greater than any individual resistor — a good sanity
check.
• Mixing this up with the parallel formula, which requires reciprocals.
• Forgetting current is the same through every series resistor, while voltage divides across them
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting E is independent of distance from an infinite sheet — a common conceptual trap
since most field formulas do fall off with distance.
• Forgetting the factor of 2, which comes from the field spreading equally to both sides of the
 sheet.
• Confusing σ (surface charge density, C/m²) with a point charge Q (in Coulombs) — different
 quantities entirely.
fields.conceptual_overview: The electric field created by an infinite, non-conducting plane sheet of uniform surface charge density $\sigma$ is spatially uniform. Its field strength depends solely on charge density and medium permittivity, remaining constant regardless of distance from the sheet
fields.real_world_applications:
Planar Semiconductor Fabrication: Modeling surface charge distributions across silicon substrate interfaces in MOSFET manufacturing.

Electrostatic Deflection Plates: Creating uniform electric fields between parallel charged plates in oscilloscope displays.
fields.jee_neet_exam_tips:
Conducting vs. Non-Conducting Sheet:Non-conducting sheet: $E = \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}$
Conducting plate (charge on two surfaces): $E = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}$
Two Oppositely Charged Parallel Plates ($\sigma, -\sigma$): Field between plates is $E = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}$; field outside is $0$.
fields.step_by_step_derivation:
Step 1: Construct a cylindrical Gaussian pillbox of cross-sectional end area $A$, extending symmetrically on both sides of the sheet
Step 2: Calculate enclosed charge:$$Q_{\text{enclosed}} = \sigma A$$
Step 3: Evaluate electric flux through the pillbox. Field vector $\vec{E}$ is perpendicular to the sheet, yielding zero flux through side walls and equal flux $E A$ through both end caps:$$\Phi_E = \oint \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{A} = E A + E A = 2 E A$$
Step 4: Apply Gauss's Law ($\Phi_E = \frac{Q_{\text{enclosed}}}{\varepsilon_0}$):$$2 E A = \frac{\sigma A}{\varepsilon_0}$$Step 5: Cancel end cap area $A$:$$E = \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}$$

fields.title: Resistors in Series
fields.variables: R = Total resistance,  R1,R2,R3 = Individual resistances
fields.description: The Total resistance(R) of a substance in series is the sum of all resistors connected in series
fields.when_to_use: When managing current division across multi-component strings
fields.mnemonic: “Series resistors just queue up and add” — no reciprocals needed, unlike parallel.
fields.example:
R1
= 4 Ω, R2
 = 6 Ω, R3
 = 2 Ω. Find R?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting series resistance is always greater than any individual resistor — a good sanity
check.
• Mixing this up with the parallel formula, which requires reciprocals.
• Forgetting current is the same through every series resistor, while voltage divides across them
fields.conceptual_overview: In a series connection, electrical components form a single unbranched path. The same electric current ($I$) passes sequentially through every resistor, while total system voltage equals the sum of individual potential drops across each component
fields.real_world_applications:
Voltage Divider Networks: Creating reference voltages in analog sensor circuits using precise series resistor ratios.

LED String Current Control: Adding series ballasting resistors to limit LED diode current and prevent thermal runaway.
fields.jee_neet_exam_tips:
Voltage Division Rule (Two Resistors):$$V_1 = V_{\text{total}} \left(\frac{R_1}{R_1 + R_2}\right)$$$N$ 
Equal Resistors ($R$):$$R_{\text{eq}} = N R$$
fields.step_by_step_derivation:
Step 1: Apply Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL) around series loop:$$V_{\text{total}} = V_1 + V_2 + V_3 + \dots$$
Step 2: Express individual voltage drops using Ohm's Law ($V_k = I R_k$):$$V_{\text{total}} = I R_1 + I R_2 + I R_3 + \dots$$
Step 3: Substitute $V_{\text{total}} = I R_{\text{eq}}$:$$I R_{\text{eq}} = I (R_1 + R_2 + R_3 + \dots)$$
Step 4: Cancel common current $I$:$$R_{\text{eq}} = R_1 + R_2 + R_3 + \dots$$

fields.title: Resistance in Parallel
fields.variables: R = Total network resistance,  R1,R2 = Individual resistances
fields.description: The Total resistance in parallel circuit is the sum of fraction of all resistors.
fields.when_to_use: When building households circuitry grids where components requires independent power loops but equal voltage
fields.mnemonic:
“Parallel resistors always end up weaker together” — total resistance is smaller than even the
smallest individual resistor.
fields.example: R1= 6 Ω, R2= 3 Ω. Find R?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting to take the reciprocal at the end — the formula directly gives $\frac{1}{R}$, not R.
• Forgetting parallel resistance is always less than the smallest individual resistor — a useful
 sanity check.
• Confusing this with the series formula, which simply adds resistances with no reciprocals at all.
fields.conceptual_overview: When electrical resistors are connected in parallel, all branches share the exact same voltage drop ($V$). Total line current splits across branches inversely proportional to branch resistance, resulting in an equivalent total resistance that is strictly smaller than the smallest individual branch resistor
fields.real_world_applications:
Residential Household Wiring: Connecting home appliances in parallel so every outlet operates independently at standard line voltage ($110\text{V}/220\text{V}$).
Current Shunt Expansion: Placing low-resistance shunts parallel to ammeters to safely measure large industrial currents.
fields.jee_neet_exam_tips: Two Resistors Shortcut:$$R_{\text{eq}} = \frac{R_1 R_2}{R_1 + R_2}$$$N$ Equal Resistors ($R$):$$R_{\text{eq}} = \frac{R}{N}$$
fields.step_by_step_derivation:
Step 1: Apply Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL) at input node:$$I_{\text{total}} = I_1 + I_2 + I_3 + \dots$$
Step 2: Express branch currents using Ohm's Law ($I_k = \frac{V}{R_k}$):$$I_{\text{total}} = \frac{V}{R_1} + \frac{V}{R_2} + \frac{V}{R_3} + \dots$$
Step 3: Substitute $I_{\text{total}} = \frac{V}{R_{\text{eq}}}$:$$\frac{V}{R_{\text{eq}}} = \frac{V}{R_1} + \frac{V}{R_2} + \frac{V}{R_3} + \dots$$
Step 4: Divide throughout by uniform potential difference $V$:$$\frac{1}{R_{\text{eq}}} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2} + \frac{1}{R_3} + \dots$$

fields.title: Joule's Law of Heating
fields.variables: H = Thermal heat energy,  I = Electric current,  R = Electric resistance,  t = Time
fields.description: The heat(H) produced in a conductor by an electric current(I) directly proportional to the square of the current (I²), the resistance (R) of the conductor, and the time (t) for which the current flows
fields.when_to_use: When analyzing electrical heating applications, calculating power transmission losses
fields.mnemonic: “Current squared, not just current” — doubling current quadruples the heat, not just doubles it.
fields.example: I = 2 A, R = 10 Ω, t = 60 s. Find H?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting the I² dependence — the single most common slip, treating heat as scaling with I
rather than I².
• Confusing total heat H (joules) with power 
(watts = $\frac{H}{t}$).
• Applying this to an ideal inductor or capacitor — it only applies to genuinely resistive heating.
fields.conceptual_overview: Joule's Law of Heating quantifies thermal energy ($H$) generated in a conductor due to electrical resistance. As charge carriers drift under an applied electric field, frequent inelastic collisions with crystal lattice ions convert electrical potential energy into microscopic kinetic vibrational heat
fields.real_world_applications:
